A record showing that a notice was received by the consumer or representative, such as a signed receipt, a certified mail receipt, or a dated entry showing hand delivery by a named staff member.

procedures: The Administrator designates [RECORDS COORDINATOR NAME] to maintain the compliance file at the licensed location, [ADDRESS]. Electronic records must be retrievable at that location during an inspection.

For each consumer, the Intake Coordinator places the following in the compliance file within 2 business days of delivery: the signed packet acknowledgment (CP-04, CP-05), the copy of the packet showing items (c)(1) through (c)(7), and the worker status disclosure.
The Intake Coordinator also files reissued pages and acknowledgments for any change of worker, hours or fees.

When services are discharged, transferred or terminated, the Administrator files a copy of the written notice with proof of delivery as described in CP-02 (10-day written notice). The file must show the date of the notice, how it was delivered, and who delivered it.
The Administrator files any report made under CP-03, including requests or offers of power of attorney, guardianship or check endorsement, and the resolution.

The Records Coordinator reviews each new consumer's compliance file within 5 business days after the first visit. Any missing item is reported to the Administrator the same day and corrected within 2 business days.

Each quarter, the Administrator audits a sample of files of consumers admitted in that quarter. The sample is the greater of five files or 10% of new admissions. For each file the Administrator checks that: the packet was delivered before the first visit; the acknowledgment is signed or the exception documented; the worker, hours and fees on the packet match the schedule and Service Agreement; the Hot Line and Ombudsman numbers are correct; the worker status disclosure is present; and no document conflicts with CP-03.
The Administrator records audit results on the audit form, with the dates, the files reviewed and findings. Corrective actions, with responsible person and due date, are tracked until completed.
Findings are reported to the Governing Body and to the quality assurance process (see GOV-04). Repeated findings trigger staff retraining.
The Administrator keeps a master index of the §611.57 compliance records so any item can be produced for the Department promptly, including during an unannounced inspection.
During any Department inspection or request, the Administrator or designee produces the requested compliance records without delay. A copy of what was produced is kept.
Compliance file records are retained under REC-01 and are protected under CR-03. They are not destroyed while a complaint, investigation or inspection is open.

responsibilities.duty: Oversee the compliance file, conduct the quarterly audit, direct corrective action and report to the Governing Body.
Maintain the file and index, check new files within 5 business days and retrieve records for inspection.
File acknowledgments, packets and disclosures on time.
Send any termination notice, delivery proof or consumer-protection concern to the Administrator promptly.

documentation: Signed packet acknowledgments and packet copies
Termination notices with proof of delivery
Worker status disclosures
Reports and resolutions under CP-03
Quarterly audit forms and corrective action tracking
Master index of §611.57 compliance records
Records of items produced to the Department

policies.title: Organization, Governing Body and Administrator Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: Owners, governing body, Administrator and management staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To define who is accountable for the operation of [AGENCY NAME] as a licensed non-medical home care agency, and how responsibilities are assigned so Chapter 611 and Chapter 51 requirements are met.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is a home care agency subject to 28 Pa. Code Chapter 611, which applies to home care agencies and registries operated in Pennsylvania, whether for-profit or nonprofit. Chapter 51 (General Information), which applies to licensed health care facilities, also applies to the agency through 28 Pa. Code §611.4(b). Chapter 611 contains General provisions (§§611.1–611.5) and Governance and Management provisions (§§611.51–611.57). The owner(s) or governing body is accountable for compliance with Chapters 611 and 51. The governing body appoints a qualified Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], who manages day-to-day operations. The agency keeps an organizational chart that shows who is responsible for hiring files, competency, tuberculosis tracking and complaints. The agency provides non-medical personal care and companionship only.

definitions.definition: The owner or owners, or the board or managing members, with ultimate legal authority over the agency.
The person appointed by the governing body to manage the agency's day-to-day operations and ensure compliance.
A current diagram naming each position, who it reports to, and the functions assigned to it.

procedures: The governing body adopts this manual and a written statement of the agency's organization, mission and non-medical scope of services. It reviews them annually (see GOV-03).

The governing body appoints the Administrator in writing. Before appointment, it confirms with the Department of Health, Division of Home Health, what qualifications are required for an Administrator, because the sources the agency reviewed conflict. The inquiry date, person spoken with and answer are put in the governance file.

Before an Administrator begins work, the governing body obtains criminal history results for the person. Under Department guidance, the results must be no more than 1 year old when the Administrator starts. The Administrator's own file is kept like a direct care worker file (see CBC-01 to CBC-03).
The governing body names an alternate to act when the Administrator is absent. The alternate's name and phone are posted in the office and given to staff.

The Administrator maintains an organizational chart that names the person responsible for hiring files and pre-hire clearances, competency evaluation and training, TB screening tracking, complaints and grievances, scheduling and supervision, billing, and records. The chart is dated and updated within 10 business days of any change.
The Administrator ensures a current copy of Chapter 611 is kept at the agency (see GEN-01) and that environmental, health and Chapter 51 requirements are met (see GEN-02).

The Administrator keeps the license current and notifies the governing body at least 120 days before the license expires so the renewal form can be submitted at least 60 days before expiration (see GOV-02).

The Administrator reports to the governing body at least quarterly on census, complaints and grievances, incidents, quality assurance results, staffing and training compliance, billing integrity and any Department contacts or inspections.
The governing body meets at least quarterly. Minutes record attendance, reports reviewed, decisions and assigned actions, and are kept in the governance file.

The governing body approves the budget, the staffing plan and any contract with a payer such as a Community HealthChoices managed care organization or the OBRA Waiver program, and ensures resources are sufficient to deliver contracted services safely.

The Administrator ensures that no one is hired, scheduled or assigned before all pre-hire and competency requirements are met (see HIR-02, CMP-01) and that supervision occurs as required (see SVC-04).
The Administrator ensures that the consumer protections in §611.57 are carried out and documented (see CP-03 to CP-06).
If the agency changes ownership or management, the Administrator and governing body follow the Chapter 51 requirements and the notification steps in GOV-02 before the change takes place.

responsibilities.duty: Remain accountable for Chapter 611 and Chapter 51 compliance, appoint and evaluate the Administrator, approve policies and budget, and meet at least quarterly.
Manage daily operations, keep the organizational chart, ensure compliance with this manual, report to the governing body and serve as primary contact for the Department of Health.
Act with the Administrator's authority when the Administrator is absent.
Carry out the functions assigned on the organizational chart (hiring files, competency, TB tracking, complaints) and report status to the Administrator.

documentation: Governing body appointment of the Administrator
Record of the confirmation with the Department regarding Administrator qualifications
Administrator's criminal history results, dated within 1 year before the start date, and other personnel file contents
Current and prior organizational charts
Governing body meeting minutes and quarterly Administrator reports
Designation of alternate Administrator

policies.title: Licensure, Service Area and Advertising Requirements
policies.applies_to: Owners, governing body, Administrator, marketing and intake staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] is licensed by the Pennsylvania Department of Health before it operates or markets, keeps that license current, and advertises and provides only the non-medical services its license allows.
policies.policy: Under 28 Pa. Code §611.2(a), no entity may operate, maintain or hold itself out as a home care agency without a Department of Health license. [AGENCY NAME] will not accept clients, provide services or advertise as a home care agency until its license is issued. Each physical location must be separately licensed. The agency does not recognize branch offices, and a virtual office does not qualify. The licensing fee and renewal fee are each $100, non-refundable and not prorated, under §611.2. The Department inspects before the initial license and before renewal, and the renewal form must be submitted at least 60 days before the license expires. Chapter 611 applies to the agency (§611.3), and Chapter 51 applies through §611.4(b), including §51.4 on change in ownership and change in management. Skilled nursing and other skilled home health care requires a separate license under 28 Pa. Code Chapter 601. [AGENCY NAME] provides non-medical personal care and companionship only, and its marketing says no more than that.

definitions.definition: An entity licensed under Chapter 611 that provides non-medical home care services to consumers through direct care workers it employs.
Advertising, marketing, or otherwise presenting oneself to the public as a home care agency, including through websites, social media, signs, directories and referral solicitations.
A separately licensed agency that provides skilled home health services. [AGENCY NAME] is not licensed to provide those services.
The actual office address licensed by the Department. A virtual office does not qualify.

procedures: Before applying, the governing body confirms the agency will have a physical office at [ADDRESS] that qualifies for licensure. The agency does not plan branch offices, and each additional location will be separately licensed.

The Administrator obtains the current application from the Department of Health, Bureau of Health Care Facilities and Home Care Services, Division of Home Health. The agency applies online only, since mailed and emailed applications ended March 31, 2026. The Administrator reconfirms the payment method for the $100 fee with the Division before submitting. The fee is non-refundable and not prorated.

The Administrator submits a complete application. The governing body budgets 2 to 5 months from a complete application to license issuance, since no official processing timeline has been verified, and does not set a service start date until the license is issued.

The Administrator keeps the Division's contact information, [DOH DIVISION PHONE, to be reconfirmed with the Division] and RA-dhhlicenquestions@pa.gov, in the governance file, and uses it to ask the Department about the application status.

The Administrator prepares the agency for the pre-licensure inspection. This includes having this manual, a current copy of Chapter 611 (GEN-01), personnel files for any staff already hired, and the consumer protection forms ready for review.

Before the license is issued, the agency does not accept clients, schedule care, advertise services, publish a website or social media page that offers care, or hand out marketing materials. Preparation such as hiring and training staff may continue as permitted by the licensing process, but no worker is assigned to a client before the license is issued.

After the license is issued, the Administrator displays the license as the Department requires and keeps a copy in the governance file. Medicaid enrollment steps with the Office of Long-Term Living, and contracting with Community HealthChoices managed care organizations, begin after licensure (see SVC-09). The agency does not bill Medicaid for services before it has been enrolled.

The Administrator calendars the license expiration date and the renewal date. The Administrator submits the renewal form and the $100 fee at least 60 days before the license expires and prepares for the renewal inspection.

Before any advertisement, brochure, website text, social media post or referral materials are published, the Administrator reviews and approves them. Materials must state only non-medical personal care and companionship services, must not claim nursing, skilled, or medical services, and must be accurate about the license and the area served.

The agency's service area is [SERVICE AREA COUNTIES]. The Intake Coordinator accepts only clients the agency can staff and supervise safely from its licensed location, and refers others to other providers or the Area Agency on Aging.

If a prospective client needs skilled nursing, therapy or other medical care, the Intake Coordinator tells the client the agency cannot provide it and refers the client to a licensed home health agency under Chapter 601. The agency may provide non-medical care alongside that care.

If the agency plans to move its office, a change in ownership or a change in management, the Administrator obtains the full text of Chapter 51 §51.4 and confirms the Department's requirements and timelines in writing with the Division before acting. Because the notice period is not stated in this policy, the Administrator records the confirmed timeline in the governance file, and the governing body calendars it. A new physical location requires a separate license.

The Administrator reports the status of licensure, renewal and any Department correspondence to the governing body at each quarterly meeting, and keeps all inspection reports, statements of deficiencies and plans of correction on file.

responsibilities.duty: Approve the licensure plan and budget, authorize no operations before licensure, and approve notice of any change of ownership, management or location.
Submit the application and renewal, prepare for inspections, approve all advertising, keep the license current and displayed, and manage Department communications.
Use only approved materials, refuse to accept clients before licensure, and refer people needing skilled care elsewhere.

documentation: Application, fee payment record and Department correspondence
Current license and prior licenses
Renewal calendar and renewal submissions
Inspection reports, statements of deficiencies and plans of correction
Approved advertising and marketing materials with approval dates
Record of Department confirmation of change-of-ownership or management notice requirements

policies.title: Policy Review and Document Control
policies.applies_to: Administrator, governing body, and all staff who use or are trained on the policy manual
policies.purpose: To keep [AGENCY NAME]'s Policy & Procedure Manual current, controlled and ready for inspection by the Pennsylvania Department of Health, and to make sure every staff member works from the current version.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will review the entire manual at least once every 12 months. It will also review the affected policies whenever 28 Pa. Code Chapter 611, Chapter 51 (which applies to licensed home care agencies under §611.4(b)), or an Office of Long-Term Living (OLTL) or Community HealthChoices MCO requirement changes. A current copy of Chapter 611 is kept at the agency office at all times (§611.4(a); see GEN-01). Every policy carries a version number and effective date, and superseded versions are archived and never discarded. The current manual is kept complete and organized so it can be produced on request for the Department's inspection before the initial license and before each renewal. Staff acknowledge in writing each policy revision that affects their duties. This policy does not use an official checklist item; it implements §611.4(a) and §611.4(b).

definitions.definition: The master version of a policy, kept by the Administrator, showing version number, effective date and approval.
A prior version of a policy that has been replaced. It is archived and marked as no longer in effect.
Any amendment to Chapter 611 or Chapter 51, or any new or changed OLTL, MCO or Department guidance, contract term or form that affects how the agency operates.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a Policy Master Index listing every policy ID, title, version number, effective date, last review date and next review due date.
Each policy shows its version (for example, v1.0), effective date, approving person and approval date in its header or footer.
By [MONTH] each year, the Administrator starts a full annual review. Each policy is assigned to a named reviewer.

Reviewers compare each policy with the current text of Chapter 611, the applicable parts of Chapter 51, and current OLTL and MCO manuals, contracts and bulletins. They record the date reviewed and the result (no change, minor revision, major revision).

The Administrator checks at least monthly for Department of Health, OLTL and MCO notices and for amendments to Chapter 611. Any change that affects a policy triggers a review of that policy within [30] calendar days, or sooner if the change has an earlier effective date.
The Administrator confirms that a complete, current copy of Chapter 611 is physically or electronically available at the agency office, and replaces it when the regulation is amended (see GEN-01).
Revised policies are approved by the Administrator and, for substantive changes, by the governing body (see GOV-01). The approval is recorded in the review log.
When a policy is revised, the version number is increased, the effective date is entered and a short change summary is added to the Policy Change Log.
The superseded version is moved to the Archive folder, marked 'SUPERSEDED' with the date, and kept for the period required in REC-01.
Within [10] business days of the effective date, the Administrator gives each affected staff member the revised policy and any needed training.
Each staff member signs and dates an acknowledgment that the revised policy was received, read and understood. The signed acknowledgments go in the personnel file (see PER-03).
New employees receive the current manual sections for their role at orientation and sign an acknowledgment before working with clients (see PER-02).

The Administrator keeps the complete current manual, the Master Index and the Policy Change Log in one place at the office, ready for inspection before the initial license and before each renewal. The Administrator reviews the manual for completeness at least 90 days before the license expiration date.
Obsolete printed copies at staff workstations or in client homes are removed and replaced when a policy changes. Electronic copies are limited to the controlled version.
If a gap is found in the manual or in how a policy is followed, the Administrator documents a corrective action with an owner and due date (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Owns the manual, runs the annual and change-triggered reviews, maintains the Master Index and Change Log, and ensures inspection readiness.
Approves substantive policy changes and receives an annual report on the review.
Compare assigned policies with current regulations and contract requirements and recommend revisions.
Read revised policies, complete assigned training, sign acknowledgments and follow the current version.

documentation: Policy Master Index
Annual Review Log with reviewer, date and outcome
Policy Change Log
Archive of superseded versions
Signed staff acknowledgments of revisions
Record of the Chapter 611 copy on file and its currency check

policies.title: Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors, and all staff involved in client service, scheduling, billing and training
policies.purpose: To monitor the quality and safety of services, find problems early, correct them, and reduce preventable harm to clients.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] operates a quality assurance and performance improvement (QAPI) program. At least quarterly, the Administrator reviews incidents, complaints, missed visits, electronic visit verification (EVV) manual-edit rates and caregiver competency reviews, looks for trends, and acts on them. Chapter 611 sets no QA committee requirement, so this program is an operator design adopted to meet the agency's quality and safety obligations. Competency is reviewed at least once each year, and more often after a caregiver is disciplined for a quality-of-care infraction (§611.55(d)-(e)). If [AGENCY NAME] knows it is out of compliance in a way that seriously compromises quality assurance or patient safety, it will immediately notify the Department of Health in writing, giving the reason and the corrective steps (28 Pa. Code §51.3(e)). For OLTL participants, the agency reports critical incidents on the Department's form, follows written prevention, reporting, notification, investigation and management procedures, gives follow-up information, and acts to reduce preventable critical incidents (55 Pa. Code §52.17(b)-(f); see SAF-02). This policy has no official checklist items.

definitions.definition: A measurable item tracked by the agency, such as missed visits, incident counts, complaints, EVV manual-edit rate and overdue competency reviews.
A known failure to meet a requirement that seriously compromises quality assurance or patient safety. It triggers immediate written notice to the Department under §51.3(e).
An event reportable for OLTL participants on the Department's critical incident form (see SAF-02).
The share of EVV visits that needed a manual correction rather than being verified electronically as delivered.

procedures: The Administrator maintains a QA Dashboard with these indicators: incidents and critical incidents, complaints and grievances, missed or late visits, EVV manual-edit rate, overdue or failed caregiver competency reviews, supervisory-visit completion, and client discharges.
Supervisors and the scheduler record data monthly in the Dashboard by the [5th] business day of the following month.

At least once every quarter, the Administrator convenes a QA review with [SUPERVISOR NAME(S)] and the person responsible for billing. The review covers all indicators for the quarter, compares them with the prior quarter and looks for patterns by client, caregiver, payer or time of day.
For each incident, the team confirms that the report was completed on time, the investigation was done, follow-up was given, and preventive steps were taken (see SAF-02).
For each complaint or grievance, the team confirms the log entry, the investigation, the response to the client and the outcome (see CR-02).
The team reviews missed visits for cause (caregiver absence, scheduling error, client refusal, no coverage) and sets actions such as backup staffing or schedule changes (see SVC-06).

The team reviews the EVV manual-edit rate by caregiver and by reason. Where the rate is high, the Administrator retrains staff and fixes the cause, such as device issues, late clock-ins or scheduling errors, aiming to meet any verified-visit threshold required by the MCOs or OLTL (see SVC-07).

The team confirms that every caregiver's competency review is current, meaning at least once per year (§611.55(d)-(e)). The Administrator schedules an additional review for any caregiver disciplined for a quality-of-care infraction, and documents it (see CMP-04).

For OLTL participants, the team reviews critical incident trends and records at least one concrete step to reduce each type of preventable incident, such as fall-risk reviews, caregiver retraining or care-plan changes (55 Pa. Code §52.17(b)-(f)).
Each identified problem is entered in a Corrective Action Plan with the problem, root cause, action, owner, due date and follow-up check. The Administrator tracks it to closure.

If the Administrator finds the agency is out of compliance in a way that seriously compromises quality assurance or patient safety, the Administrator notifies the Department of Health in writing immediately. The notice gives the reason for the noncompliance and the corrective steps being taken (§51.3(e)). The Administrator keeps a copy of the notice and tracks the corrective steps to completion.
The Administrator checks at least quarterly whether any issue found in the review meets the serious noncompliance standard, and records the decision.
The Administrator records minutes of each QA review, with attendees, findings, decisions and assigned actions, and signs them.
The Administrator reports QA results and open corrective actions to the governing body at least [quarterly/semi-annually] (see GOV-01).
Findings that show a policy is unclear or not working are sent to the policy review process (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Leads the QAPI program, makes the written notice to the Department when required, and tracks corrective actions to closure.
Supply indicator data, complete supervisory visits and competency reviews, and carry out corrective actions.
Track missed visits and EVV manual edits and report causes.
Reviews QA reports and ensures resources for corrective action.

documentation: QA Dashboard
Quarterly QA review minutes
Corrective Action Plans
Competency review records and additional reviews after discipline
Critical incident follow-up and prevention records
Copies of any written notice to the Department under §51.3(e)

policies.title: Corporate Compliance, Fraud and Billing Integrity
policies.applies_to: Owners, Administrator, billing and scheduling staff, supervisors and all caregivers
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] bills Medicaid and other payers only for services that were actually delivered, authorized and verified, and to prevent, detect and correct fraud, waste and abuse.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] bills Medicaid only for verified, authorized visits. Medicaid personal assistance services (PAS) are paid through the Community HealthChoices MCOs (the CHC program operates under a 1915(b) waiver, with a 1915(c) waiver application pending) and through OLTL under the OBRA Waiver, according to each contract. Medicaid personal care visits must be captured in electronic visit verification (EVV), as required by 42 USC 1396b(l) and Pennsylvania's EVV implementation, in effect since January 1, 2020. Visits are not billed if they were not delivered or verified, and manual EVV edits are used only for documented, legitimate reasons. [AGENCY NAME] screens workers and owners against exclusion lists and confirms the specific list and frequency requirements with each MCO and OLTL. The agency may serve OBRA Waiver participants only once it is enrolled through OLTL, and will not promise or start Medicaid services for a client before enrollment with the payer is complete. This policy has no official checklist items.

definitions.definition: Billing for services not delivered, upcoding or inflating hours, falsifying records, billing for unauthorized services, and other practices that cause improper payment.
Electronic visit verification: the electronic record of the service type, client, caregiver, date, and start and end times of a visit.
A government list of individuals or entities barred from participating in Medicaid or other federal health programs.
A Community HealthChoices managed care organization that authorizes and pays for PAS under its contract.
A correction to an EVV record made after the visit rather than captured automatically.

procedures: The Administrator is the Compliance Officer unless the governing body designates another person in writing: [COMPLIANCE OFFICER NAME].

Before billing any Medicaid payer, the Administrator confirms that the agency is enrolled with the payer (the CHC-MCO or OLTL for the OBRA Waiver) and holds the required Pennsylvania license. Intake staff do not tell any client or referral source that Medicaid-funded service is available until enrollment is complete (see SVC-09).
For each Medicaid client, intake staff obtain and file the written authorization showing the service, units or hours, dates and any limits. They schedule only within the authorization.
Caregivers record each Medicaid personal care visit in the EVV system at the start and end of the visit, at the client's home, and perform only the authorized services (see SVC-07).

Billing staff bill only visits that were delivered, verified in EVV and within the authorization. Before submitting claims, they reconcile EVV data, timesheets and the authorization, and hold any claim that does not match.

A manual EVV edit requires a written reason, the caregiver's attestation and supervisor approval. The Administrator does not approve edits made only to produce a billable visit. Manual edits are tracked monthly and reviewed under GOV-04, with the aim of keeping them within any verified-visit threshold set by the MCOs or OLTL.

Before hire or contracting, and at least [monthly] after, the Administrator screens every caregiver, supervisor, owner, officer and billing employee against the exclusion lists the MCOs and OLTL require. Until the MCOs and OLTL confirm their lists, the agency includes the federal HHS-OIG List of Excluded Individuals/Entities and the Pennsylvania Medicheck list in its screening. The date, result and person screening are recorded.
A worker or owner who appears on an exclusion list is removed immediately from all Medicaid-funded work and the Administrator contacts the affected payers as their contracts require.

The Administrator confirms the screening requirements, billing rules, record-retention periods and audit procedures in each MCO and OLTL contract and provider manual at enrollment and at least annually. Changes are sent through GOV-03.
Overpayments identified by the agency or a payer are reported to the payer and returned as the contract requires, with a record of the date, amount and cause.
Each employee receives compliance training at orientation and annually, covering false billing, EVV integrity, gifts and kickbacks, and how to report concerns (see PER-02).

Anyone may report a suspected compliance problem to the Compliance Officer, or to the Administrator or governing body if the concern involves the Compliance Officer. Reports may be made anonymously through [REPORTING METHOD]. No one is retaliated against for a good-faith report.
The Compliance Officer investigates each report within [10] business days, stops any improper billing, corrects claims, imposes discipline and documents the outcome in the Compliance Log.

The Compliance Officer conducts a documented internal audit at least quarterly of a sample of Medicaid claims against authorizations, EVV records and visit notes, and reports results to the governing body (see GOV-04).
The agency cooperates fully with payer, OLTL, state and federal audits and requests for records, and keeps billing and service records for the period in REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Runs screening, audits, investigations and training, and reports to the governing body.
Bill only verified, authorized visits and hold mismatches.
Schedule within authorization and approve manual EVV edits only when properly documented.
Use EVV accurately and report concerns.
Oversees compliance and reviews audit results.

documentation: Payer authorizations
EVV records and manual-edit log with reasons and approvals
Exclusion screening log
Quarterly claim audit reports
Compliance Log of reports and investigations
Overpayment refund records
Compliance training attendance records
Payer enrollment confirmations

policies.title: Client Rights and Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: All clients (private pay and Medicaid), intake staff, supervisors and caregivers
policies.purpose: To make sure every client knows and can exercise their rights, understands their responsibilities, and receives services with dignity, choice and protection from improper practices.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives every client a written Client Rights and Responsibilities statement with the information packet before services begin (§611.57(c); see CP-04 and CP-05). The statement includes the rights in §611.57(a): the client may take part in service planning and receive services with reasonable accommodation of their needs and preferences, and will receive at least 10 calendar days' written notice before termination of services. Shorter notice applies only if the client is over 14 days in arrears or worker safety is at risk. The statement also tells the client that no one affiliated with the agency may assume power of attorney or guardianship over the client, and that the agency may not require the client to endorse checks over to it (§611.57(b)). The statement tells the client how to reach the Department of Health complaint Hot Line (1-866-826-3644, to be confirmed per CP-05) and the local Area Agency on Aging Ombudsman (§611.57(c)). Medicaid participants also receive the additional participant rights required by their MCO or OLTL, and for Medicaid home and community-based services the agency supports person-centered planning and the participant's choices under 42 CFR 441.301(c). Staff explain the rights in a language and format the client understands and document that they did so. This policy has no official checklist items.

definitions.definition: A person who receives or has applied to receive services from [AGENCY NAME].
Adjusting services, schedules, communication or methods, within the agency's scope, to fit a client's documented needs and preferences.
The easy-to-read packet given before services begin (see CP-04 and CP-05).
A person the client chooses or who is legally authorized to act for the client. No one affiliated with the agency may serve as the client's power of attorney or guardian.

procedures: The Administrator maintains the current Client Rights and Responsibilities statement in plain, easy-to-read language and in the languages most used by the agency's clients (see CR-05).

The statement lists these rights: to be treated with dignity and respect; to take part in service planning; to receive services with reasonable accommodation of needs and preferences; to be free from abuse, neglect, exploitation and discrimination; to privacy and confidentiality; to be told about services, hours, fees and total costs before services begin; to know who the assigned worker is; to refuse services; to make a complaint without retaliation; and to have at least 10 calendar days' written notice before termination.

The statement also says the agency and its owners, employees and contractors may not take power of attorney or guardianship over a client, and the agency may not require the client to endorse checks over to it.
The statement includes the agency's contact details, the Department of Health complaint Hot Line (1-866-826-3644) and the local Area Agency on Aging Ombudsman number, as set out in CP-05.
Before services begin, the intake coordinator or supervisor gives the client (and representative, if any) the statement together with the information packet, and reads or explains it.

Staff use the client's preferred language or an interpreter, large print or other accommodation as needed (see CR-05). They ask the client to say in their own words what the main rights are, to check understanding.
The client or representative signs and dates an acknowledgment of receipt. If the client cannot or will not sign, the staff member notes the reason, the date and the witness.
The signed acknowledgment, the language used and the name of the person who explained the rights are filed in the client record (see REC-01).

For Medicaid clients, the intake coordinator also gives the rights statements and notices required by the client's MCO or OLTL, and confirms the specific content with the payer at enrollment and annually (see SVC-09).

The statement lists the client's responsibilities: give accurate information, tell the agency of changes in health, schedule or contact details, treat caregivers with respect, provide a safe workplace, follow the agreed service plan, pay fees as agreed (private pay), and give notice of cancellations.
Supervisors review the rights with the client again at the start of each plan update and at least annually (see SVC-03, SVC-04) and note the review in the record.
Caregivers are trained at orientation on client rights and are told that any suspected violation must be reported to the supervisor the same day (see PER-02).
Any report of a rights violation is entered in the complaint log and handled under CR-02. Allegations of abuse, neglect or exploitation are handled under SAF-01.
If the agency proposes to end services, the supervisor follows CP-02, including at least 10 calendar days' written notice unless the client is over 14 days in arrears or worker safety is at risk.
The Administrator reviews the statement at least annually and whenever Chapter 611, OLTL or MCO requirements change (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Keeps the rights statement current and compliant, and addresses violations.
Gives and explains the statement before services begin, obtains the acknowledgment and documents the language used.
Respect client rights and report suspected violations the same day.
Follows the stated responsibilities and raises concerns.

documentation: Current Client Rights and Responsibilities statement and version history
Signed acknowledgment of receipt
Record of language, interpreter or format used
Annual rights review notes
Payer-required Medicaid rights notices
Complaint log entries related to rights

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All clients and representatives, supervisors, the Administrator and all staff
policies.purpose: To give clients a clear, safe way to raise concerns, and to make sure each complaint is recorded, investigated, resolved and used to improve services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] welcomes complaints and does not retaliate against anyone who makes one. Before services begin, the client packet tells each client how to complain to the agency, to the Department of Health complaint Hot Line (1-866-826-3644; confirm the number per CP-05) and to the local Area Agency on Aging Ombudsman (§611.57(c)). The client may complain at any time, including about services, workers, billing or a notice of termination (§611.57(a)). The agency logs, investigates and resolves each complaint, and reviews the log for trends. Community HealthChoices participants may also use their MCO's grievance process, and the agency confirms timelines with each MCO. This policy has no official checklist items.

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction or concern about the agency or its staff, made orally or in writing, whether or not the client calls it a complaint.
A complaint, including one filed with an MCO, that goes through a formal review process.
Any adverse action, such as reducing hours, changing caregivers without consent, threatening discharge or treating the client differently, because a client or representative complained.
The local Area Agency on Aging long-term care ombudsman, an independent advocate.

procedures: The information packet and the rights statement tell each client how to complain to [AGENCY NAME] ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE], [ADDRESS]), to the Department of Health complaint Hot Line (1-866-826-3644) and to the local Area Agency on Aging Ombudsman, with the Ombudsman's local telephone number (see CP-05). Staff tell the client the client may contact any of these at any time.
Staff explain the complaint process to the client orally at intake, in a language the client understands, and note it in the record (see CR-01, CR-05).

Any staff member who receives a complaint, oral or written, records it the same day on a Complaint Form, including the date, client, complainant, person involved, details and requested outcome, and gives it to the Administrator by the next business day. Staff may not discourage a complaint or ask the client to withdraw it.
The Administrator assigns a case number and enters the complaint in the Complaint Log.
The Administrator acknowledges the complaint to the client by phone or in writing within [2] business days.

If the complaint alleges abuse, neglect, exploitation, a health or safety risk, or a critical incident, the Administrator immediately follows SAF-01 and SAF-02 and takes any needed protective action, such as removing the caregiver from the case pending investigation.

The Administrator, or a supervisor not involved in the matter, investigates promptly by interviewing the client, caregiver and others, and reviewing visit notes, EVV data and the service plan. The investigation is completed within [14] calendar days unless there is a documented reason for more time.

The Administrator gives the client a written or oral response within [14] calendar days of the complaint, stating the findings, the action taken and the client's further options, including the Department of Health Hot Line and the Ombudsman. The client may disagree and ask for review by the governing body.

For a CHC participant, the Administrator also tells the participant of the right to use the MCO's grievance and appeal process, and gives the MCO's contact information. The agency confirms current MCO timelines and notice requirements and cooperates with any MCO review (see SVC-09).

No retaliation is allowed. The supervisor monitors the client's services for [90] days after a complaint, including by calling the client, to confirm no adverse treatment. Retaliation by any employee is grounds for discipline up to termination (see PER-05).
The Administrator records the outcome, corrective action, response date and client satisfaction in the Complaint Log.
At least quarterly, the Administrator reviews the Complaint Log for trends by caregiver, issue, client or payer and enters corrective actions in the QA program (see GOV-04).
The Administrator reports unresolved or recurring complaints to the governing body (see GOV-01).
Complaint records are kept in a separate file and in the client record as required in REC-01. Complaint information is kept confidential (see CR-03).
If the Department of Health or another agency contacts [AGENCY NAME] about a complaint, the Administrator cooperates, provides requested records promptly and documents the contact.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the process, investigates or assigns investigation, responds to clients and maintains the log.
Receive complaints, escalate them, monitor for retaliation and carry out corrective actions.
Accept and report every complaint without discouraging or retaliating.
Reviews unresolved or recurring complaint patterns.

documentation: Complaint Forms
Complaint Log with dates, findings and outcomes
Investigation notes
Written responses to clients
Retaliation monitoring notes
Quarterly trend review minutes
Information packet and rights acknowledgment showing complaint contacts were given

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers and anyone with access to client or worker information
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy and confidentiality of client, worker and applicant information, and to comply with HIPAA where it applies.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] protects the confidentiality of client and worker information. Confidentiality is a required competency topic that every direct care worker must be tested or trained on before assignment (§611.55(b)(1); see CMP-02). If [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity, for example because it bills Medicaid using standard electronic transactions, it will comply with the HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164), including the administrative requirements of 45 CFR 164.530. The agency will confirm its covered-entity status with counsel before it begins billing, and will treat all client information in the same careful way whether or not HIPAA applies. The agency designates a Privacy Officer and trains all staff at orientation. Criminal history information obtained on applicants and workers is kept confidential, as required by Chapter 611 and set out in CBC-03. This policy has no official checklist items.

definitions.definition: Information about a client's health, care or payment that identifies the client, in any form: paper, electronic or oral.
A health plan, clearinghouse or health care provider that transmits health information electronically in connection with standard HIPAA transactions.
The person designated by the agency to develop and oversee privacy policies and handle privacy complaints (45 CFR 164.530).
An unauthorized acquisition, access, use or disclosure of PHI that compromises its security or privacy.
The least amount of information needed to accomplish a purpose.

procedures: The governing body designates a Privacy Officer, [PRIVACY OFFICER NAME], who is responsible for privacy and security, receives privacy questions and complaints, and oversees breach response. The designation is documented in writing.

Before billing any payer electronically, the Administrator confirms with counsel whether [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity, and records the determination. If it is, the agency completes a security risk analysis and adopts written HIPAA privacy and security procedures.
If the agency is a covered entity, it gives each client a Notice of Privacy Practices at the first service delivery, makes a good-faith effort to get a signed acknowledgment, and keeps the record.

At orientation and before working with any client, each employee is trained on confidentiality, what counts as client information, and the rules below, and signs a confidentiality agreement (see PER-02). Training is repeated at least annually and when procedures change. Training dates are kept in the personnel file.

Staff access client information only when needed for their job and disclose only the minimum necessary. They do not discuss clients in public places, on social media or with anyone not involved in care.

The agency releases client information only with the client's written authorization, or as permitted or required by law, such as for payment, treatment coordination, abuse reporting (see SAF-01), required reports to the State (see REC-02), and oversight by the Department of Health, OLTL or an MCO. Each non-routine disclosure is logged.

Client records are kept in locked files or in password-protected systems with role-based access, unique user IDs, automatic log-off and audit logging. Paper records are not left in vehicles or unattended.

Caregivers who use phones or EVV apps do not keep client information on personal devices except in the approved application. They do not photograph clients or records, or text identifiable client information.
Records are disposed of only by shredding or secure deletion, after the retention period in REC-01.

Clients may ask to see their records, get copies, request corrections and ask for an accounting of certain disclosures. The Privacy Officer responds within the time required by law, and in any case within [30] days, and documents the response.
Staff who suspect a privacy incident, such as a lost device, misdirected message or unauthorized access, tell the Privacy Officer the same day.

The Privacy Officer investigates, limits the harm and decides whether it is a reportable breach. If it is, the agency makes the notifications required by law and by payer contracts, within the legally required times, and records the facts and outcome.

Criminal history reports, ChildLine results and similar worker screening information are kept in a secure file separate from general personnel records, and access is limited to those who need it (see CBC-03).

Clients and workers may file a privacy complaint with the Privacy Officer or the Administrator. No one will be retaliated against for filing (see CR-02). Employees who violate this policy are subject to discipline, up to termination (see PER-05).
The Privacy Officer reviews this policy and privacy practices at least annually and sends revisions through GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees privacy and security, training, access requests, breach response and complaints.
Confirms covered-entity status, provides resources and enforces the policy.
Protect client information, sign the confidentiality agreement, complete training and report incidents.
Designates the Privacy Officer and oversees compliance.

documentation: Privacy Officer designation
Covered-entity determination
Signed confidentiality agreements
Training records
Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgments (if covered entity)
Disclosure log
Access and amendment request records
Security risk analysis (if covered entity)
Privacy incident and breach investigation records

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All employees, direct care workers, supervisors, contractors and anyone affiliated with [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect consumers' money, property and legal independence, and to prevent financial exploitation of consumers by anyone affiliated with [AGENCY NAME].
policies.policy: No one affiliated with [AGENCY NAME] may assume power of attorney or guardianship over a consumer, and the agency will never require a consumer to endorse checks over to it (28 Pa. Code §611.57(b)). Staff may not borrow from, lend to, or sell to consumers. Staff may not accept gifts above the agency's limit, and may never accept cash, checks or gift cards. Staff may not hold or use a consumer's bank, debit or credit cards, PINs or passwords. Money handled for an errand must be authorized by the consumer, receipted and documented. Staff must report suspected financial exploitation immediately under SAF-01, as required by the Older Adults Protective Services Act (35 P.S. §10225.701) and the Adult Protective Services Act (Act 70 of 2010). Agency gift limit: gifts of nominal value only, with a maximum of $20 in value per occasion and never money or its equivalent. The governing body may change this limit through GOV-03.

definitions.definition: The unauthorized, improper or deceptive use or taking of a consumer's money, property or resources for someone else's benefit, including coercing a consumer to give, lend or sign over assets.
A legal authority to act for a consumer in financial or personal matters. No one affiliated with the agency may hold it for a consumer.
Cash or other funds the consumer gives a worker for a specific purchase, such as groceries or a pharmacy pickup, that the consumer has authorized.
A small, non-cash item of $20 or less per occasion, such as a baked good or a card, that does not create an obligation or favor.

procedures: At hire and annually, the Administrator trains every employee on this policy and on the exploitation indicators listed in SAF-01. Training is documented in the personnel file (PER-03).
Each employee signs an acknowledgment that they may not accept power of attorney, guardianship, representative payee or similar authority for any consumer.

If a consumer, family member or third party offers such a role to staff or to the agency, the worker declines and tells the supervisor the same day. The supervisor records the offer and refers the consumer to an independent source, such as family, an attorney or the Area Agency on Aging.

The agency will not ask a consumer to endorse checks, including Medicaid or insurance payments, over to the agency. Private-pay consumers pay by methods the consumer chooses and set out in the service agreement (CR-06).
Staff may not borrow money or property from consumers, lend money to them, buy or sell items to or from them, or ask for loans, gifts, tips or bequests.

If a consumer offers a gift, the worker declines politely. If the gift is a non-cash item of nominal value ($20 or less) and refusing would cause real distress, the worker may accept it once. The worker reports it to the supervisor within one business day for entry on the Gift Log.

Gifts of cash, checks, gift cards, jewelry, vehicles or property, and any gift over $20, are always declined. A worker who is named in a consumer's will or asked to change one must report this to the Administrator immediately.
Staff may not hold, carry or use a consumer's ATM, debit or credit card, checkbook, PIN or online passwords. Staff may not add themselves to a consumer's account.
Before any errand involving money, the worker confirms the consumer's authorization and amount. The consumer's service plan (SVC-03) must list shopping and errands as a task.

For each errand, the worker completes an Errand Money Record. It shows the amount received, items purchased, change returned and the receipts attached. The consumer signs the record when able, and the worker keeps funds and the consumer's money separate from their own.
Supervisors review Errand Money Records at each supervisory visit (SVC-04). The agency investigates any discrepancy and reports it under SAF-01.
Workers do not move, store, sell or discard a consumer's valuables except at the consumer's direction. Workers report any missing or damaged consumer property to the supervisor the same day.
On a report of missing property or money, the supervisor documents it on an incident report (SAF-02), notifies the Administrator, and informs the consumer of the right to contact law enforcement.

Any employee with reasonable cause to suspect financial exploitation of a consumer age 60 or older must immediately make an oral report to the local Area Agency on Aging, as required by 35 P.S. §10225.701. For a consumer age 18 to 59 with a disability, the employee reports to the statewide Adult Protective Services line, 1-800-490-8505 (24/7). Follow SAF-01 for the full steps and written follow-up.
The agency does not retaliate against staff who report in good faith. The Administrator may suspend a worker from the consumer's home while an allegation is reviewed.
The Administrator reviews the Gift Log and Errand Money Records quarterly and reports trends to the governing body under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Approves this policy and the gift limit, and receives quarterly reports.
Trains staff, investigates reports and takes corrective action. Ensures the agency never accepts power of attorney or requires check endorsement.
Reviews errand records and the Gift Log, responds to reports and initiates reporting under SAF-01.
Decline prohibited gifts and loans, document errand money, and report suspected exploitation immediately.

documentation: Employee acknowledgment of this policy (personnel file)
Errand Money Records with receipts
Gift Log entries
Incident reports for missing property or money (SAF-02)
Copies of reports made to the Area Agency on Aging or the Adult Protective Services line (SAF-01)
Training records

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All employees, direct care workers, supervisors, contractors, applicants for service and consumers of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To ensure that every consumer and applicant is treated without discrimination, that people with limited English proficiency can understand and use the agency's services, and that people with disabilities receive reasonable accommodation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate against any consumer or applicant on the basis of race, color or national origin, in accordance with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 USC 2000d), which applies to programs receiving federal financial assistance such as Medicaid. The agency also does not discriminate on the basis of disability and provides reasonable accommodation as required by the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). The agency will not discriminate on the basis of age, sex, religion, sexual orientation, gender identity, or source of payment in accepting or serving consumers, except as the payer's authorization or the agency's service area and staffing capacity require. The agency provides interpreter and translation services at no cost to consumers with limited English proficiency, and offers the consumer information packet in the consumer's language.

definitions.definition: A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English well enough to communicate about services.

A person who is fluent in English and the consumer's language, understands the relevant terminology, and interprets accurately and impartially. A bilingual staff member is qualified only if assessed as competent for this role.

A modification to the way services are provided or communicated that lets a person with a disability take part in and benefit from services, unless it would cause undue burden or fundamentally alter the service.
Aids that make communication effective for people with hearing, vision or speech disabilities, such as sign language interpreters, large print, Braille or captioning.

procedures: At intake (SVC-02), the intake coordinator asks every applicant for their preferred spoken and written language and any communication needs. The answers are recorded on the intake form and in the client record.

Staff do not make acceptance decisions or assign workers based on race, color, national origin or disability. A consumer's request for a worker of a particular gender or language is handled as a care preference under CP-01, and the supervisor documents it.

When a consumer has limited English proficiency, the supervisor arranges a qualified interpreter, in person or by telephone or video interpreter service, for intake, assessment, service planning, rights explanations, supervisory visits and grievances. There is no charge to the consumer.

The agency does not require consumers to provide their own interpreter. A family member or friend may interpret only if the consumer requests it, and the supervisor records that choice. A minor child may not interpret except in an emergency until a qualified interpreter is available.

The agency offers the consumer information packet, service agreement, rights notice and grievance procedure in the consumer's language, through a translated version or through oral interpretation with a written record that this was done. See CP-04, CP-05 and CR-06.
The packet must give the DOH complaint Hot Line (1-866-826-3644) and the Area Agency on Aging Ombudsman number. Make sure these numbers are clearly communicated to LEP consumers.

For consumers who are deaf or hard of hearing, or who have vision, speech or cognitive disabilities, the supervisor identifies appropriate auxiliary aids, such as large print or a sign language interpreter, and arranges them before the first visit.

When a consumer or applicant with a disability requests an accommodation, the supervisor records the request. The supervisor works with the consumer to find an effective option, documents it in the service plan (SVC-03), and tells the assigned worker.

If a requested accommodation cannot be provided, the Administrator reviews the request, considers alternatives with the consumer, and documents the reason in writing. The consumer is told of the right to file a grievance (CR-02).
Where possible, the agency assigns a worker who speaks the consumer's language. If none is available, the supervisor arranges interpretation support and a written or pictorial task list.

Staff may not make derogatory remarks, use slurs, or refuse to serve a consumer because of race, color, national origin or disability. Violations are handled under PER-05 and may result in discipline up to termination.

The agency posts and gives consumers a notice explaining that language assistance and accommodations are free and how to ask for them. It states that the consumer may file a grievance with the agency (CR-02) or a complaint with outside agencies, including the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights.
Supervisors record each use of interpreter services, including the date, language and method, in the client record (REC-01).
All staff are trained at orientation and annually on this policy, working with interpreters, and respectful communication with people with disabilities (PER-02).

The Administrator reviews this policy annually with legal counsel to confirm it reflects current federal and state requirements, and reviews complaints and language-assistance logs for trends (GOV-03, GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Oversees compliance, contracts for interpreter and translation services, decides on accommodation disputes and reviews the policy annually.
Records language and communication needs at first contact and arranges interpretation for intake.
Arranges interpreters, auxiliary aids and accommodations, and documents them.
Treat all consumers respectfully, use interpreter services as arranged, and report discrimination or unmet communication needs.

documentation: Intake record of preferred language and communication needs
Accommodation requests and responses in the service plan
Interpreter use log
Record of translated materials or oral interpretation of the information packet and agreements
Training records
Grievances alleging discrimination and their resolution (CR-02)

policies.title: Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: Administrator, intake staff, billing staff, supervisors and all consumers (private-pay, Community HealthChoices and OBRA Waiver)
policies.purpose: To make sure every consumer receives and signs a clear written service agreement before services begin that states the services, worker, hours, fees, total costs, billing terms and termination notice rule.
policies.policy: Before services begin, [AGENCY NAME] gives each consumer an easy-to-read written service agreement that states the services to be provided, the worker who will provide them, the hours of service, and the hourly or weekly fees and total costs (28 Pa. Code §611.57(c)(1)-(3)). The agreement also states minimum hours, cancellation and billing terms, and the termination notice rule. The consumer must receive at least 10 calendar days' written notice before termination. A shorter notice applies only if the consumer is more than 14 days in arrears or the worker's safety is at risk (§611.57(a)). For Medicaid consumers, the agreement states that the managed care organization (MCO) or program pays the agency, and the consumer owes no additional charge unless it is authorized. The consumer's signature is obtained before the first visit.

definitions.definition: The signed written agreement between the consumer and [AGENCY NAME] that describes services, worker, hours, fees, total costs and terms of service.
The full amount the consumer can expect to pay for the services and hours in the agreement for a billing period, including any minimum-hour charges and other fees.
Fees owed to the agency that have not been paid by their due date. For notice purposes, more than 14 days past due.
A Community HealthChoices managed care organization that pays the agency for authorized Medicaid personal assistance services.

procedures: After intake and assessment (SVC-02), the intake coordinator prepares the service agreement from the consumer's service plan and, for Medicaid consumers, from the payer authorization.
The agreement lists the services to be provided, using the task list in the service plan (SVC-03) and the in-scope services in SVC-01.
The agreement identifies the assigned worker by name. It states that the agency will notify the consumer of any change in worker, and that the consumer may ask for a different worker.
The agreement states the days and hours of service, as scheduled under SVC-06.

For private-pay consumers, the agreement states the hourly rate or weekly fee, any rate differences (such as holidays, overnights or weekends), minimum hours per visit or week, and the estimated total cost for the stated schedule. All fees must be listed. The agency may not charge a fee that is not in the signed agreement.

The agreement states the billing method and cycle, due dates, accepted payment methods, late-payment terms and what happens when payment is returned. The agency does not require the consumer to endorse any check over to the agency (§611.57(b); CP-03).

The agreement states the cancellation terms: how much notice the consumer must give to cancel or change a visit, and any charge that applies for late cancellation. If no charge applies, the agreement says so.

The agreement states the termination notice rule. The agency or the consumer must give at least 10 calendar days' written notice to end services. A shorter notice applies only if the consumer is more than 14 days in arrears or a worker's safety is at risk. See CP-02.

For CHC and OBRA consumers, the agreement states that the MCO or program pays the agency for authorized services. It states that the consumer owes no extra charge for authorized services unless it is lawfully authorized, and it lists any consumer cost-sharing required by the payer. Coordination with the payer follows SVC-09.

If the consumer chooses to buy additional private-pay hours beyond the Medicaid authorization, the supervisor prepares a separate private-pay section or agreement with its own rates and totals. It must be signed separately and must state that the additional hours are voluntary.

The intake coordinator reviews the agreement with the consumer, or the consumer's chosen representative, in plain language and in the consumer's language (CR-05). The coordinator answers questions and gives the consumer a copy of the information packet (CP-04, CP-05).
The consumer signs and dates the agreement before the first visit. An agency representative signs and dates it. The agency gives the consumer a complete signed copy.

No one affiliated with the agency may sign as the consumer's power of attorney or guardian (§611.57(b); CP-03). A consumer's family member or legally authorized representative may sign only with the representative's authority verified, and the agency records it.

When services, hours, worker or fees change, the supervisor issues a written amendment before the change takes effect (except for emergency changes) and obtains the consumer's signature. Fee increases require written notice to the consumer before they apply.
Billing staff send invoices that match the signed agreement and verified visit records (SVC-07). They investigate and correct any error, and refund any overcharge promptly.
The Administrator reviews the agreement template annually (GOV-03) and files each signed agreement in the client record (REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the agreement template and rate schedule and ensures no consumer starts services without a signed agreement.
Prepares and reviews the agreement with the consumer and obtains signatures.
Bill only as stated in the agreement and verified visits, and correct errors.
Issues amendments when service details change and confirms workers are those named in the agreement.

documentation: Signed service agreement and any amendments
Signed receipt of the information packet (CP-04, CP-05)
Written fee schedule
Payer authorization for Medicaid consumers
Invoices, payment records and refund records
Written notices of termination (CP-02)

policies.title: Scope of Services: What Caregivers May and May Not Do
policies.applies_to: All direct care workers, supervisors, intake staff and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To define the non-medical personal care, instrumental activities of daily living (IADL) and companionship services that [AGENCY NAME] provides under its Chapter 611 license, and to keep workers from performing skilled tasks that require a separate Chapter 601 license.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides non-medical services only: personal care, IADLs and companionship services, as those terms are defined in 28 Pa. Code §611.5. IADLs are defined by section 802a of the Health Care Facilities Act (35 P.S. §448.802a). Companionship services are socialization, support and IADL help. Personal care includes help with bathing, toileting, transfers, meals and assistance with self-administered medication, as covered in the competency content of §611.55(c). Caregivers may assist consumers with self-administered medications (§611.55(c)(6)). Caregivers may not perform skilled nursing tasks. Skilled home health care requires a separate license under 28 Pa. Code Chapter 601, which [AGENCY NAME] does not hold. The agency maintains a written list of tasks that are in and out of scope. Workers must refuse, or escalate to the supervisor, any request outside scope.

definitions.definition: An individual employed by or referred through the agency who provides direct consumer contact in the consumer's home, as defined in §611.5.
A person who receives services from the agency, as defined in §611.5.
The consumer's right to direct how, when and by whom services are provided, as the term is used in §611.5.

Activities that support living independently at home and in the community, as defined by section 802a of the Health Care Facilities Act (35 P.S. §448.802a) and incorporated in §611.5. Examples include meal preparation, shopping, light housekeeping, laundry and help with transportation and telephone use. The statutory definition controls.
Socialization, support and IADL help, as defined in §611.5.
Hands-on, non-medical help with activities such as bathing, toileting, transfers and meals, and assistance with self-administered medication.

A task that requires the judgment or training of a licensed nurse (an RN or LPN, as defined in §611.5) or another licensed clinician, and that may be provided only by a Chapter 601 home health agency or other properly licensed provider.

procedures: The Administrator maintains the written In-Scope / Out-of-Scope Task List. The list is reviewed annually under GOV-03 and given to every worker at orientation (PER-02).

In-scope services are: (a) personal care: bathing, toileting, transfers, dressing, grooming, meal assistance, and reminders and assistance with self-administered medications as limited by SVC-05; (b) IADLs: meal planning and preparation, shopping and errands, light housekeeping, laundry and help with telephone use or appointments; and (c) companionship: socialization, supervision and support.

Out-of-scope services include skilled nursing tasks such as: giving injections; wound or ulcer care; ostomy, catheter or tube-feeding care beyond non-skilled hygiene; administering, drawing up, adjusting or deciding on medications; assessing or interpreting vital signs or symptoms for treatment; oxygen or ventilator adjustment; and therapy services. The supervisor consults the Chapter 601 license limits and the list when in doubt.

Workers also may not give medical advice, change a consumer's diet or treatment, or perform tasks the consumer is not authorized to direct. They may not provide services for anyone in the household other than the consumer, except as the agreement allows.

During intake and assessment (SVC-02), the supervisor screens every requested task against the task list. Requests that are skilled in nature are referred to the consumer's physician, Service Coordinator, MCO or a licensed home health agency.
The service plan (SVC-03) lists each authorized task. The worker is given the written task list and may perform only the tasks on it.

Medication assistance is limited to help with self-administered medications, such as reminding, opening containers, handing the consumer the container or the medication, and observing the consumer take it. The worker may not decide dose or timing. See SVC-05.

When a worker receives a request outside scope from a consumer, family member or other provider, the worker politely declines, explains that the agency's license does not allow the task, and calls the supervisor the same day.

The supervisor documents the request, explains the limit to the consumer, and arranges an appropriate referral. If the consumer needs skilled care, the supervisor tells the consumer or representative and the Service Coordinator, and does not continue the skilled task.
If a worker is unsure whether a task is in scope, the worker does not perform it until the supervisor answers. An on-call supervisor is reachable at [PHONE].
In an emergency, workers follow SVC-08: call 911, stay with the consumer, and notify the supervisor. Summoning emergency help is never out of scope.

Workers who perform an out-of-scope task are retrained, and repeated or serious violations lead to discipline under PER-05. Skilled tasks done in error are reported on an incident report (SAF-02) and reviewed by the Administrator.

Orientation and annual training cover the scope list and the core and personal care content required by §611.55: confidentiality, consumer control, IADLs, changes in the consumer, infection control, universal precautions, emergencies, documentation, abuse and neglect reporting, difficult behaviors, bathing, toileting, transfers, meals and self-administered medication assistance (CMP-02, CMP-03).
The agency's advertising and consumer information must describe services only as non-medical (GOV-02). The Administrator reviews materials for any language implying skilled care.
If the agency wishes to offer skilled home health services in the future, it will first apply for a separate Chapter 601 license. Until the license is issued, no skilled services will be offered.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the task list, ensures services stay within the Chapter 611 license, and decides unclear scope questions.
Screens requests at intake, writes the task list into each service plan, answers workers' scope questions and arranges referrals.
Perform only authorized in-scope tasks, decline or escalate out-of-scope requests, and document services.
Explains the agency's non-medical scope to applicants and refers skilled needs elsewhere.

documentation: Written In-Scope / Out-of-Scope Task List and revision history
Service plan task list for each consumer
Record of out-of-scope requests and referrals
Worker acknowledgment of the task list
Training records on scope and §611.55 competency content
Incident reports for out-of-scope tasks performed in error (SAF-02)

policies.title: Client Intake, Eligibility and Assessment
policies.applies_to: Intake coordinator, supervisors, billing staff and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To ensure that each consumer's needs, payer, authorization and eligibility are verified, and that an assessment and the required information packet are completed before services begin.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] completes intake and a needs assessment before services begin. The agency verifies the payer and authorization. It does not start Medicaid services without a valid authorization. Medicaid personal assistance services are paid through the Community HealthChoices (CHC) managed care organizations (MCOs) and, once the agency is enrolled through the Office of Long-Term Living (OLTL), through the OBRA Waiver. The agency asks at intake whether any consumer is under 18, which triggers the ChildLine rules in CAC-01. Before the first visit, the agency delivers the information packet required by 28 Pa. Code §611.57(c).

definitions.definition: The process of receiving a referral or inquiry, collecting basic information, and deciding whether the agency can safely and appropriately serve the person.
A review of the consumer's non-medical needs, functional abilities, preferences, home environment and safety risks that guides the service plan.
The payer's approval, including the services, hours and dates, that allows the agency to provide and bill for Medicaid services.
Community HealthChoices, Pennsylvania's capitated Medicaid managed care program through which MCOs pay agencies for personal assistance services.
A Pennsylvania Medicaid home and community-based waiver administered by OLTL. The agency may serve OBRA participants only once enrolled through OLTL.

procedures: The intake coordinator records every inquiry or referral on the Intake Form on the day received. It records the consumer's name, contact information, location, requested services, referral source, payer and language needs (CR-05).

The coordinator confirms the consumer lives inside the agency's licensed service area (GOV-02) and that staffing is available. If the agency cannot serve the person, the coordinator documents the reason and refers the person to other providers.

The coordinator confirms the consumer's payer: private pay, a CHC MCO or the OBRA Waiver. For Medicaid consumers, the coordinator obtains the Service Coordinator's contact information and the authorization or service plan from the MCO or program.

The agency does not begin Medicaid services without a valid authorization showing the services, hours and dates. The billing staff verifies the authorization and the consumer's eligibility with the MCO or program before scheduling, and records the verification date.

The agency serves OBRA Waiver participants only after OLTL enrollment is complete. Until then, the coordinator tells OBRA applicants that the agency cannot yet serve them and helps them find an enrolled provider.
The coordinator asks whether anyone to be served is under 18. If so, the coordinator refers the case to the Administrator for the ChildLine requirements in CAC-01 before any worker is assigned.

The coordinator screens the request against the scope of services in SVC-01. Skilled needs are referred to a licensed provider. The agency does not accept a consumer whose needs it cannot safely meet with non-medical services.

A supervisor completes an in-home needs assessment before services begin, with the consumer, and the consumer's representative if the consumer wishes. The assessment covers functional abilities, personal care and IADL needs, medications the consumer self-administers, cognitive and communication needs, behaviors, home and safety risks, emergency contacts and consumer preferences.

The supervisor looks for risks to the worker and the consumer, including pets, smoking, firearms, hazards and unsafe conditions (SAF-05). Any concern is documented and discussed with the Administrator before services start.
The supervisor invites the consumer to take part in planning and records preferences and reasonable accommodations (CP-01, CR-05).
The supervisor develops the service plan from the assessment and, for Medicaid consumers, from the authorized plan (SVC-03).
