Before the first visit, the coordinator delivers the easy-to-read information packet required by §611.57(c): services and identity of the worker, hours, fees and total costs, Department of Health contact, the DOH complaint Hot Line 1-866-826-3644, the local Area Agency on Aging Ombudsman number, and hiring and competency requirements (CP-04, CP-05). The consumer signs a receipt.

The service agreement is reviewed and signed before the first visit (CR-06). The consumer also receives the rights and responsibilities notice and the grievance procedure (CR-01, CR-02) and the privacy notice (CR-03).
The supervisor assigns a worker who has completed all hiring and competency requirements (HIR-02, CMP-01) and informs the consumer of the worker's name.

The coordinator opens the client record (REC-01) with the intake, authorization verification, assessment, signed packet receipt, service agreement and service plan. The first visit may not occur until all of these are complete.

responsibilities.duty: Approves intake criteria, ensures no Medicaid services start without authorization, and handles ChildLine cases and OLTL enrollment.
Receives referrals, verifies the service area, collects information, asks about consumers under 18 and delivers the packet.
Performs the in-home assessment, develops the service plan and assigns an eligible worker.
Verifies payer eligibility and authorization before services are scheduled.

documentation: Intake Form and referral records
Payer and authorization verification, with date and initials
Needs assessment and risk screening
Record of the question about consumers under 18 and any CAC-01 follow-up
Signed receipt of the §611.57(c) information packet
Service agreement and service plan
Declined-referral log with reasons

policies.title: Service Plan and Plan Updates
policies.applies_to: Supervisors, intake staff, direct care workers and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To ensure each consumer has a written service plan developed with the consumer's participation, followed by workers, and updated when needs change.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] builds each service plan with the consumer's participation and preferences, as 28 Pa. Code §611.57(a) provides, and delivers services with reasonable accommodation of the consumer's needs and preferences. For Community HealthChoices (CHC) and OBRA Waiver consumers, the agency follows the plan authorized by the Service Coordinator, consistent with the person-centered planning requirements for home and community-based services at 42 CFR 441.301(c). The agency updates the plan on any change in the consumer's condition or needs. Each assigned worker receives the written task list before providing services.

definitions.definition: The written plan that lists the consumer's needs and preferences, the services and tasks to be performed, the schedule, the assigned worker and any accommodations.
A plan developed with the consumer, reflecting the consumer's goals, preferences and strengths, as required for Medicaid home and community-based services under 42 CFR 441.301(c).
The CHC-MCO or program staff member responsible for developing and authorizing the Medicaid consumer's person-centered service plan.
The written list of the specific tasks a worker is to perform for a consumer at each visit, drawn from the service plan.

procedures: After the needs assessment (SVC-02), the supervisor drafts the service plan. For a private-pay consumer, it is based on the assessment and the consumer's stated needs. For a CHC or OBRA consumer, it follows the plan and authorized services from the Service Coordinator.

The supervisor meets with the consumer, and the consumer's chosen family member or representative if the consumer wishes, to develop the plan. The consumer is asked what tasks are most important, when and how care should be done, and preferences for gender, language, routines and cultural or religious practice (CP-01).

The plan lists the specific tasks within the scope of SVC-01, the days and hours, the assigned worker, and the consumer's preferences and accommodations. It must not include tasks outside the agency's scope.

For Medicaid consumers, the supervisor compares the plan against the authorization to make sure the tasks and hours do not exceed what is authorized (SVC-09). If the consumer needs more services than authorized, the supervisor contacts the Service Coordinator.

The plan identifies risks and safety measures from the assessment, such as fall risk, emergency contacts, behaviors and home hazards (SAF-04, SAF-05), and includes instructions for what the worker should do in each situation.
The consumer reviews the plan and signs it, or the supervisor documents the consumer's agreement. The consumer receives a copy. The consumer's participation and any disagreement are recorded.

Before the worker's first visit, the supervisor reviews the written task list with the worker, explains the consumer's preferences and accommodations, and has the worker sign that they have received it.
The worker follows the task list and consumer control rules at every visit. The worker records the tasks completed (SVC-07, REC-01) and does not add or drop tasks without the supervisor's direction.

The supervisor reviews the plan at supervisory visits (SVC-04) and at least every [90] days for private-pay consumers. For CHC and OBRA consumers, the supervisor reviews it when the Service Coordinator reassesses and at any time the authorized plan changes.

The supervisor updates the plan promptly, no later than the next scheduled visit, when a worker, family member or the consumer reports a change in condition (SVC-08), a hospitalization, a change in needs, preferences or home situation, or a change in the authorization.

A significant change, such as a decline needing skilled care, is reported to the consumer's physician, representative or Service Coordinator, as appropriate, and documented. The agency never delays notification.

Updates to hours, tasks or worker are made in writing, communicated to the consumer and worker the same day, and, when the fees or hours change, reflected in an amendment to the service agreement (CR-06).
When the Service Coordinator issues a revised authorized plan, the supervisor replaces the task list, notifies the worker, and files the new plan with the date received.
The Administrator audits a sample of plans quarterly to verify consumer participation, authorization match and timely updates (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Develops and updates the plan with the consumer, reviews it with the worker and monitors implementation.
Follow the written task list, honor the consumer's preferences, and report changes in condition or need.
Obtains the authorized plan from the Service Coordinator for Medicaid consumers.
Audits plans for compliance and consumer participation.

documentation: Service plan with consumer signature or documented agreement
Authorized plan from the Service Coordinator (CHC and OBRA)
Worker's signed receipt of the task list
Plan update and review notes with dates
Records of communications with the consumer, representative and Service Coordinator about changes
Quarterly plan audit results

policies.title: Supervision of Caregivers and Supervisory Visits
policies.applies_to: All direct care workers (caregivers), provisional hires, the Administrator, and any supervisor or care coordinator employed or designated by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every caregiver is supervised, observed in the home and re-evaluated for competency on a defined schedule. The schedule gives particular attention to provisional hires and to workers disciplined for a quality-of-care infraction. It also ensures consumer feedback is collected and acted on.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supervises every caregiver through a designated supervisor. Chapter 611 sets no supervisor-to-worker ratio, so the supervision schedule in this policy is the agency's own design. The agency will meet or exceed the Chapter 611 minimums. (1) Each caregiver's competency is reviewed through direct observation at least once per year, and more often after discipline for a quality-of-care infraction (28 Pa. Code §611.55(e)). (2) Provisional hires receive more frequent documented random observation, and the agency obtains consumer feedback on them, as a condition of provisional hiring (28 Pa. Code §611.54(a)). (3) Consumer feedback is requested at every supervisory contact. Supervision stays within non-medical personal care and companionship. No official Department checklist item is assigned to this policy.

definitions.definition: The Administrator or a staff member designated in writing by the Administrator to observe, coach, evaluate and document caregiver performance.
An in-home visit or direct observation of a caregiver delivering services, with consumer feedback sought during or right after the visit.
A documented review in which the supervisor watches the caregiver perform assigned tasks and rates the caregiver against the competency topics in CMP-02 and CMP-03.
A caregiver working before all required reports are received, under the conditions in PRV-01 and PRV-02.
A substantiated failure to deliver services safely or as planned, such as neglect of a task, unsafe technique, a confidentiality breach or a boundary violation that affects care.

procedures: The Administrator designates in writing each supervisor and the caregivers assigned to that supervisor. The supervisor list is reviewed at least quarterly and whenever staffing changes.

The Administrator sets caseload limits so every supervisor can complete the visits below on time. If a supervisor falls behind on required visits, the Administrator reassigns caregivers or adds supervisory capacity.
At hire, the supervisor reviews the caregiver's competency documentation (see CMP-04) and confirms that competency was established before the caregiver's first assignment (see CMP-01).

For every new caregiver-client assignment, the supervisor makes a first supervisory contact within 14 days of the first visit. This is the agency's design standard. The supervisor observes the caregiver in the home, reviews the service plan with the caregiver and consumer, and asks the consumer for feedback.

After the first contact, the supervisor makes a supervisory visit or consumer contact at least every 90 days for each active assignment, or sooner if the service plan, the consumer or a complaint calls for it.

For provisional hires, the supervisor performs documented random direct observation at least once in the first 7 days of service and at least every 14 days afterward until all required reports are received or the provisional period ends (28 Pa. Code §611.54(a)). The supervisor also collects consumer feedback at each observation. Time limits and termination are in PRV-02.

At each supervisory visit, the supervisor compares the care delivered with the written service plan (see SVC-03) and checks that the caregiver follows infection-control practice, the scope-of-services limits in SVC-01 and the medication-assistance limits in SVC-05.

At each visit the supervisor asks the consumer or representative specific feedback questions. These cover satisfaction, punctuality, respect, whether the plan is being followed, and any concern or change in condition. The supervisor records the answers in the consumer's own words where practical.

At least once every 12 months, the supervisor completes a direct-observation competency review for every caregiver. The review covers the topics in CMP-02 and, for caregivers who provide personal care, CMP-03 (28 Pa. Code §611.55(e)). The supervisor completes the annual review before the 12-month anniversary of the last review.

If a caregiver is disciplined for a quality-of-care infraction, the supervisor repeats the direct-observation competency review within 30 days of the discipline. The supervisor then repeats observation at the interval the Administrator sets in writing, until the Administrator documents that performance is acceptable (28 Pa. Code §611.55(e)).

If a visit shows unsafe practice, the supervisor corrects it immediately, retrains the caregiver on the specific task, and documents the retraining. If a consumer is at risk, the supervisor removes the caregiver from the assignment and notifies the Administrator the same day.

If a supervisory visit uncovers possible abuse, neglect, exploitation, a reportable event or a critical incident, the supervisor stops and follows SAF-01 and SAF-02 immediately and notifies the Administrator.
If the consumer reports a complaint at a visit, the supervisor records it and opens a grievance under CR-02. The supervisor does not ask the consumer to wait for the next visit.

The supervisor files each visit note and competency review in the caregiver's personnel file (see PER-03) and records consumer feedback in the client record (see REC-01). Both are completed within 3 business days of the visit.

The Administrator reviews monthly a report of overdue supervisory visits, overdue annual competency reviews, provisional-hire observations and consumer feedback trends, and reports the results to the quality assurance program (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Designates supervisors, sets caseloads, approves the post-discipline observation plan, reviews overdue-visit reports monthly and ensures supervision is carried out.
Conducts supervisory visits, direct-observation competency reviews and provisional-hire observations on schedule, collects consumer feedback, retrains caregivers and documents all activity.
Cooperates with observation, follows coaching and retraining, and reports concerns to the supervisor.
Schedules visits so supervisors can observe caregivers and tracks due dates for annual reviews.

documentation: Supervisory visit notes with date, caregiver, consumer, observations and consumer feedback
Annual direct-observation competency review forms
Post-discipline competency re-review records
Provisional-hire observation log with consumer feedback
Retraining and corrective-action records
Monthly overdue-visit and supervision report
Written supervisor designations and caregiver assignment list

policies.title: Medication Assistance and Self-Administration Support
policies.applies_to: All direct care workers (caregivers), supervisors and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To define the limited, non-medical help caregivers may give with medications the client takes on their own, to prohibit administration of medications, and to set steps for reporting refusals, errors and reactions.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is licensed as a non-medical home care agency under 28 Pa. Code Chapter 611. Skilled home health care requires a separate license under Chapter 601, which the agency does not hold. Caregivers may assist only with medications that the client self-administers. Caregivers must be trained in this assistance before they provide it, because medication assistance is a required competency topic for workers who provide personal care (28 Pa. Code §611.55(c)(6)). Caregivers may not administer medications, set or change doses, or give injections. Any refusal, error or adverse reaction is reported at once to the supervisor and to the client's prescriber or family. A medication error that causes death or serious injury is a reportable event under 28 Pa. Code §51.3 (see SAF-02). No official Department checklist item is assigned to this policy.

definitions.definition: A medication the client takes or applies by their own action, directing it themselves or through a family caregiver, while the caregiver provides only permitted assistance.

Reminding the client it is time to take a medication, bringing the client their container or water, helping open a container the client has selected, steadying the client's hand, and observing and recording what the client reports taking. The client or family member selects and takes the medication.

Deciding which medication or how much to take, measuring or changing doses, placing medication in the client's mouth, giving injections, applying medicated treatments that require clinical judgment, or any other act reserved for licensed or authorized persons.
A missed dose, wrong medication, wrong dose, wrong time or wrong person, or any deviation from the prescriber's directions that the caregiver observes or learns of.

procedures: Before a caregiver provides any medication assistance, the supervisor confirms the caregiver completed training on assistance with self-administered medications and that this is documented in the competency file (see CMP-03 and CMP-04).

At intake and assessment, the supervisor determines whether the client can self-administer medications and records who fills the pillbox or sets up medications (the client, a family member or a licensed professional). The agency does not set up medications (see SVC-02).

The service plan states exactly what medication help, if any, the caregiver will give, such as verbal reminders or opening a container, and who is responsible for the medications. The client or representative agrees to this in writing (see SVC-03).
The caregiver follows the plan. The client or family member chooses the medication and decides to take it. The caregiver may remind, bring, open and steady, and then observe.

The caregiver never sets or changes a dose, never crushes, splits or mixes medications, never gives an injection, and never gives a medication from an unlabeled container or a container not labeled for the client.

If the client asks for help beyond what is allowed, the caregiver politely declines, explains that the agency cannot do it, and calls the supervisor. The supervisor arranges another solution with the client or family, such as a family member or a licensed professional.

After a medication reminder, the caregiver records on the visit record the date, time, which medication task was assisted and whether the client took it or refused. The caregiver records only what the client reports or what the caregiver saw.

If the client refuses a medication, the caregiver does not argue or force it. The caregiver records the refusal and notifies the supervisor right away, the same day and before leaving the visit if possible.

The supervisor notifies the client's prescriber or the family or representative of a refusal, according to the client's wishes recorded in the service plan. The supervisor documents who was notified, the time and the response.

If the caregiver notices or suspects a medication error, such as a missed dose or the client taking the wrong medication, the caregiver stays with the client, calls the supervisor immediately and follows the supervisor's instructions.
If the client has an adverse reaction, such as difficulty breathing, swelling, fainting, a seizure or other signs of an emergency, the caregiver calls 911 first and then the supervisor (see SVC-08).
For any refusal, error or reaction, the supervisor notifies the client's prescriber or family the same day, documents the notification, and checks that the client has been seen or advised as needed.

The supervisor reports to the Administrator the same day any error causing death or serious injury. The Administrator determines whether the event is reportable under 28 Pa. Code §51.3, confirms the report timing in the full text of that section, and files the report under SAF-02. For OLTL participants, the Administrator also applies the critical incident steps in SAF-02.

The caregiver completes a written incident statement within 24 hours. The supervisor reviews the circumstances, retrains the caregiver if a task was done incorrectly, and refers repeated or serious problems for discipline under PER-05.

The supervisor checks medication assistance practice at supervisory visits (see SVC-04), and the Administrator reviews medication events at least quarterly in the quality assurance program (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Keeps services within the Chapter 611 non-medical scope, decides reportability of serious medication events, files reports and reviews medication events for quality assurance.
Confirms training, defines the medication help in the service plan, handles refusal and error notifications to the prescriber or family and documents them.
Provides only permitted assistance, never administers, records what occurs and reports refusals, errors and reactions immediately.
Selects and takes medications, arranges for medication set-up, and tells the agency of changes in medications.

documentation: Caregiver training and competency record for assistance with self-administered medications
Service plan section on medication assistance, with client or representative agreement
Visit records noting medication reminders, assistance and refusals
Medication refusal, error and reaction notifications, with who was notified and when
Incident reports and caregiver written statements
Reports filed under SAF-02, when required
Retraining and corrective-action records

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
policies.applies_to: Scheduler/care coordinator, on-call coordinator, supervisors, caregivers and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every client knows their hours and who is coming, that visits are covered even when a caregiver is unavailable, and that every missed visit is logged, explained and reported as required.
policies.policy: Before services begin, [AGENCY NAME] gives each consumer in the information packet the hours of service and the identity of the assigned worker (28 Pa. Code §611.57(c)(1)-(2); see CP-04). The agency keeps a backup caregiver pool and an on-call coordinator so that scheduled visits are covered. Every missed visit is logged with its cause and the notice given to the client. For Community HealthChoices (CHC) participants, MCOs may expect monthly reporting of missed personal assistance services visits. The agency will confirm the requirement in each MCO's provider manual or contract and report as required. No official Department checklist item is assigned to this policy.

definitions.definition: A scheduled visit that does not occur, begins more than 60 minutes late without the client's agreement, or ends substantially short of the scheduled time without the client's agreement.
Qualified caregivers who have completed all pre-hire and competency requirements and are available to cover visits when the assigned caregiver cannot.
The staff member reachable by phone outside office hours, including nights, weekends and holidays, who arranges coverage and responds to client and caregiver calls.
Consistent assignment of qualified caregivers and prompt coverage so that the client's services under the service plan are not interrupted.

procedures: Before services begin, the scheduler records the client's authorized or agreed hours, days and tasks from the service plan and confirms them with the client or representative (see SVC-03 and CR-06).
Before the first visit, the scheduler gives the client the hours of service and the name of the assigned caregiver in the information packet or in writing (28 Pa. Code §611.57(c)(1)-(2); see CP-04).
The scheduler assigns only caregivers who have met all hiring, clearance and competency requirements (see HIR-02 and CMP-01), and matches caregivers to client needs, preferences and travel distance.
The scheduler keeps a roster of backup caregivers and an on-call coordinator schedule, posted weekly. The on-call number, [PHONE], is given to every client and caregiver.

A caregiver who will be late or cannot work a shift notifies the scheduler or on-call coordinator as soon as known, and at least 4 hours before the shift when possible. The caregiver does not arrange a substitute independently.

When a caregiver is absent, the scheduler or on-call coordinator immediately assigns a backup caregiver and informs the client of the change and the substitute's name. Substitutes must meet the same requirements as regular caregivers.

If no caregiver is available, the coordinator calls the client or representative before the scheduled start time, explains the situation, and offers the earliest alternative time or another solution. The coordinator documents the conversation.

If a visit is missed, the coordinator contacts the client within 1 hour of discovering it to find out whether the client is safe and whether urgent needs exist. If the client cannot be reached and safety is a concern, the coordinator follows SVC-08.

The coordinator enters every missed visit in the missed visit log the same day. The entry records the date, client, scheduled caregiver, scheduled time, cause (for example caregiver illness, no-show, client unavailable, weather or transportation), when and how the client was notified, and makeup or backup coverage arranged.

If the client or family declines, cancels or is unavailable, the scheduler records that cause and the notice received, and informs the supervisor if it happens repeatedly or suggests a change in the client's condition.
The supervisor reviews any pattern of missed visits by caregiver or client at least monthly, counsels caregivers about repeated late arrivals or no-shows under PER-05, and reassigns staff as needed.

For CHC participants, the Administrator confirms in each MCO's provider manual or contract whether monthly missed PAS visit reporting is required and what format and deadline apply. When it is required, the scheduler prepares the report from the missed visit log and the Administrator reviews and submits it on time.

Any missed visit that places a client at risk, or that the Administrator believes is a critical incident for an OLTL participant, is handled under SAF-02, including notice to the participant's Service Coordinator within 24 hours.

When a caregiver is permanently reassigned or leaves, the scheduler notifies the client in advance where possible, introduces the new caregiver, and gives the client the new worker's identity before the first visit.
The Administrator reviews missed visit totals, causes and backup coverage success at least quarterly in the quality assurance program (see GOV-04). Corrective actions are documented.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures adequate backup coverage and on-call arrangements, confirms MCO reporting requirements, submits required reports and reviews missed visit trends.
Schedules qualified caregivers, informs clients of hours and worker identity, assigns backups, contacts clients about missed visits and keeps the missed visit log.
Is reachable outside office hours, arranges emergency coverage and responds to client safety concerns.
Reviews patterns of missed visits and counsels or reassigns caregivers.
Arrives on time, gives prompt notice of lateness or absence and does not arrange substitutes independently.

Notice to client of hours and worker identity before services begin
Backup caregiver roster and on-call schedule
Missed visit log with cause and notice given
Client contact notes about missed visits and makeup coverage
Monthly missed visit reports for CHC MCOs, when required, and confirmation of the MCO requirement
Quality assurance review of missed visits

policies.title: Electronic Visit Verification and Timekeeping
policies.applies_to: Caregivers, scheduler, payroll and billing staff, supervisors and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every Medicaid personal care visit is captured through electronic visit verification (EVV), that manual edits are kept to a minimum and justified, and that visit times are recorded accurately for billing and payroll.
policies.policy: Medicaid personal care visits must be captured in EVV. EVV has been in effect in Pennsylvania since January 1, 2020, under the federal requirement in 42 USC 1396b(l). [AGENCY NAME] captures every Medicaid PAS visit in EVV, whether the participant is in Community HealthChoices (CHC) or the OBRA Waiver. A secondary source reports an 85% verified-without-manual-edit threshold, with quarterly alerts from January 2026. The agency will confirm the current threshold and reporting with each MCO and OLTL, and it sets 85% as its internal target. CHC plans use the HHAeXchange system, according to the vendor's site, and the agency will confirm the system and set-up with each MCO. Private-pay visits are not billed to Medicaid but are timed and recorded under the same timekeeping practices. No official Department checklist item is assigned to this policy.

definitions.definition: An electronic system that records the type of service, the individual receiving it, the individual providing it, the date, and the location, start time and end time of each visit.
A change or addition to an EVV visit record made after the visit, rather than a record captured live at the point of service.
A visit captured live in EVV that matches the schedule and location and has no manual edit.
The record of hours worked used for payroll and billing, which must match the EVV record for Medicaid visits.

procedures: Before enrolling in any Medicaid program, the Administrator confirms with each CHC-MCO and with OLTL the EVV system the agency must use, the registration steps and any training, and records the answers in the EVV file.

Before a caregiver works a Medicaid visit, the scheduler or payroll staff registers the caregiver and the participant in the EVV system and confirms that the schedule and authorized services are loaded correctly.

New caregivers are trained on EVV use during orientation (see PER-02). Training covers how to check in and out, what to do when the system or phone fails, and why accurate times matter. The training is documented.

At the start of each Medicaid visit, the caregiver checks in using the approved EVV method, in the client's home, and checks out at the end of the visit. The caregiver never checks in or out for another person and never from outside the client's home unless an approved method requires it.

A caregiver who cannot check in or out because of a technology problem calls the scheduler or on-call coordinator right away. The caregiver records the actual start and end times and the reason for the problem.

The scheduler corrects an EVV record only when a legitimate reason exists, such as a device failure, a missed check-out or a documented schedule change. Each manual edit includes the reason code, the actual times worked, the name of the person who made the edit and the date.

Staff never edit EVV records to increase billing, to hide a late arrival or a missed visit, or to match the schedule. Falsifying a visit record is a violation of the corporate compliance policy (see GOV-05) and results in discipline up to termination.
Payroll staff pay caregivers from actual hours worked as recorded in the verified visit or the documented edit, and compare EVV times with timekeeping records every pay period (see PER-04).

Billing staff submit Medicaid claims only for visits that are captured in EVV and match the authorized service and the units billed. Billing staff hold any claim that has an unresolved EVV discrepancy until the discrepancy is corrected and documented.
The scheduler runs the EVV exception report each week, covering missed check-ins, late check-ins, visits with edits and unmatched visits, and resolves each item within 5 business days.
Each month the Administrator reviews the rate of visits verified without manual edit, in total and by caregiver. The agency's internal target is at least 85%, subject to confirmation with the MCO.

A caregiver with frequent manual edits receives retraining from the supervisor within 14 days of the monthly review. The retraining and any follow-up are documented, and repeated problems are handled under PER-05.

The Administrator checks at least quarterly with each MCO for EVV alerts, thresholds and compliance reports. The Administrator confirms the current standard in writing and updates this policy if the requirement changes.
When a participant is hospitalized, absent or otherwise unavailable during a scheduled visit, the caregiver or scheduler records it as a missed visit under SVC-06 and does not bill for the visit.
EVV records, edit logs, exception reports and payroll reconciliations are kept for the period required in REC-01 and made available to OLTL, the MCOs and auditors on request.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms EVV requirements and thresholds with MCOs and OLTL, reviews monthly edit rates and ensures compliance.
Registers caregivers and participants, loads schedules, reviews weekly exceptions and documents legitimate edits.
Reconcile EVV and timekeeping records, pay actual hours worked and bill only verified or properly edited visits.
Retrains caregivers with frequent edits and monitors accurate visit recording.
Checks in and out live at each visit, reports technology problems immediately and never falsifies times.

documentation: EVV registration and system confirmation with each MCO and OLTL
Caregiver EVV training records
EVV visit records and manual-edit log with reasons
Weekly exception reports and their resolution
Monthly verified-without-manual-edit rate report
