MCO and OLTL EVV alerts and correspondence

policies.title: Change in Client Condition and Emergencies in the Home
policies.applies_to: All direct care workers (caregivers), supervisors, on-call coordinator and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure caregivers recognize and report changes in a client's condition, respond to emergencies by calling 911 first, and that reportable events and critical incidents are escalated to the right agencies on time.
policies.policy: Recognizing changes in the consumer and handling emergencies are required competency topics for every caregiver (28 Pa. Code §611.55(b)(4) and (b)(7)). In an emergency, the caregiver calls 911 first and then the supervisor. Caregivers do not diagnose or treat. They observe, report and get help. A hospital transfer resulting from injury or accident is a reportable event under 28 Pa. Code §51.3. For participants in OLTL programs, critical incidents are reported as described in SAF-02, consistent with the OLTL Critical Incident Management Bulletin. No official Department checklist item is assigned to this policy.

definitions.definition: Any noticeable difference in the client's physical, mental, emotional or functional status, appetite, mobility, skin, behavior, sleep, continence or safety in the home.

A situation that threatens life, health or safety and needs immediate help, such as unresponsiveness, chest pain, trouble breathing, stroke signs, serious bleeding, a serious fall or injury, fire, or a threat of violence or self-harm.

An event listed in 28 Pa. Code §51.3 that must be reported to the Department, including an unusual-circumstance death, a medication-error death or serious injury, a hospital transfer from injury or accident, an abuse complaint, rape, a disaster disruption, loss of vital utilities and unlicensed practice.
An incident defined in the OLTL Critical Incident Management Bulletin involving a participant in the CHC Waiver, OBRA Waiver or Act 150, reported under the OLTL process.

procedures: During orientation and annually, each caregiver is trained to recognize and report changes in the consumer and to respond to emergencies, and the training is documented (28 Pa. Code §611.55(b)(4) and (b)(7); see CMP-02).

The supervisor records in the service plan each client's emergency contacts, physician or prescriber, known medical conditions, advance directive or emergency preferences the client has shared, and the preferred hospital. The caregiver has quick access to this information during each visit.
At each visit, the caregiver observes and notes any change in condition, such as new confusion, weakness, pain, falls, skin changes, appetite changes, refusal of care or changes in mood or behavior.

For a non-urgent change, the caregiver records it on the visit record and calls the supervisor the same day. The supervisor contacts the client or family, advises them to contact the client's physician, and documents the contact. The supervisor reviews whether the service plan needs revision (see SVC-03).
In an emergency, the caregiver calls 911 first and gives the address, the client's condition and what happened. The caregiver then calls the supervisor or on-call coordinator at [PHONE].

While waiting for help, the caregiver stays with the client, keeps the client safe and comfortable, and follows only the basic first aid and universal precautions learned in training (see SAF-03). The caregiver does not give medication, food or drink if the client may be seriously ill, and does not move a client who may be injured unless there is immediate danger.

The caregiver gives emergency responders the client's medication list, emergency contacts and physician information if available, and does not leave the client alone until responders take over. If the client is taken to the hospital, the caregiver does not ride along unless approved by the supervisor.
The supervisor or on-call coordinator notifies the client's family or representative of the emergency as soon as possible and informs the Administrator within 1 hour.

The caregiver completes a written incident statement the same day or by the end of the shift. The statement includes the date, time, what was observed, what was done, who was called and when, and the outcome.

The Administrator decides, the same day, whether the event is a reportable event under 28 Pa. Code §51.3, for example a hospital transfer from injury or accident or a death under unusual circumstances. The Administrator confirms the required report timing in the full text of §51.3 and files the report under SAF-02.

If the client is a participant in the CHC Waiver, OBRA Waiver or Act 150, the Administrator determines whether the event is a critical incident under the OLTL bulletin. If it is, the agency notifies the participant's Service Coordinator within 24 hours of discovering it and submits the first section of the critical incident report within 48 hours, as set out in SAF-02.
If the emergency involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, the caregiver and supervisor follow SAF-01 in addition to this policy.

If a client dies while in service, the caregiver calls 911 and the supervisor, does not disturb the scene beyond emergency efforts, and the Administrator handles notifications and any required reports under SAF-02.

After an emergency, the supervisor reviews the event with the caregiver within 3 business days. If it is clinically appropriate and the client agrees, the supervisor updates the service plan and notifies the Service Coordinator or MCO care manager for Medicaid participants (see SVC-09). The supervisor also provides support to a caregiver affected by the event.
The Administrator reviews all changes in condition and emergency events at least quarterly in the quality assurance program to identify trends and training needs (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Determines reportability under §51.3 and OLTL requirements, files reports on time and reviews emergency events for quality improvement.
Receives caregiver reports, notifies family or representatives and the Administrator, follows up on changes in condition and updates the service plan.
Observes and reports changes, calls 911 first in emergencies, stays with the client, follows training and documents the event.
Provides current emergency contacts and medical information and tells the agency about changes.

documentation: Caregiver training records on changes in condition and emergencies
Emergency contact and physician information in the service plan
Visit records noting changes in condition
Caregiver incident statements
Supervisor notes on family, physician and Service Coordinator notifications
Reports filed under SAF-02, including §51.3 reports and OLTL critical incident reports
Post-event review and service plan updates

policies.title: Coordination with Medicaid Programs and Payers
policies.applies_to: Administrator, intake and billing staff, supervisors and care coordinators of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To set how [AGENCY NAME] works with Community HealthChoices (CHC) managed care organizations (MCOs), the OBRA Waiver and OLTL so that Medicaid participants receive coordinated services, incidents reach the Service Coordinator on time, and the agency meets payer requirements.
policies.policy: State licensure under 28 Pa. Code Chapter 611 comes first. The OLTL waiver enrollment step follows licensure. [AGENCY NAME] does not accept Medicaid participants until it is licensed and enrolled or contracted for the relevant program. CHC is a capitated Medicaid managed-care program operating under a 1915(b) waiver with a 1915(c) waiver application, and agency personal assistance services (PAS) under CHC are paid through the CHC-MCOs. The OBRA Waiver was renewed effective July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2031, and the agency may serve OBRA participants once enrolled through OLTL. The agency follows the participant's person-centered service plan, as required for home and community-based services under 42 CFR 441.301(c), and captures Medicaid visits in EVV (see SVC-07; 42 USC 1396b(l)). The agency notifies the participant's Service Coordinator within 24 hours of discovering a critical incident, and failure to do so can bring DHS or OLTL sanctions up to termination of the provider contract. The agency asks each CHC-MCO about credentialing and rates (HCPCS W1793), and its network status with each MCO is not assumed until confirmed in writing. No official Department checklist item is assigned to this policy.

definitions.definition: Pennsylvania's capitated Medicaid managed long-term services and supports program, administered by OLTL and delivered through CHC-MCOs.
A managed care organization contracted with the Commonwealth to arrange and pay for CHC services, including agency PAS.
The Medicaid home and community-based waiver administered by OLTL, serving eligible participants under an approved renewal effective July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2031.
The person (employed by the MCO or another entity) who coordinates a participant's services and to whom the agency reports critical incidents and service changes.
The billing code for agency personal assistance services, used in CHC and related Medicaid rate schedules.
An event defined in the OLTL Critical Incident Management Bulletin that providers in the CHC Waiver, OBRA Waiver and Act 150 must report.

procedures: The Administrator does not apply for Medicaid enrollment, and does not accept Medicaid referrals, until the Chapter 611 license is issued (see GOV-02). After licensure, the Administrator contacts the OLTL enrollment and certification unit and follows its steps for OBRA Waiver and other OLTL provider enrollment.

The Administrator contacts each CHC-MCO serving the agency's service area to ask about credentialing requirements, contracting, the PAS rate for HCPCS W1793 and billing and EVV requirements. The Administrator records each answer, with the date and name of the person who gave it, in the payer file.

The agency treats its network status with each MCO as unconfirmed until it holds a signed contract or written credentialing confirmation. It does not tell any referral source or client that it is in-network before that confirmation.

Before accepting a Medicaid referral, intake staff verify the participant's eligibility and the program (CHC or OBRA), the authorized service, the number of hours or units, the authorization period and the Service Coordinator's name and contact information (see SVC-02).

The agency provides services as described in the participant's person-centered service plan and authorization, and its own service plan is consistent with them (see SVC-03). Supervisors do not change authorized hours or tasks without approval from the Service Coordinator or the MCO.

When a change in the participant's needs or condition occurs, such as a hospitalization, a decline in function or a request for more or fewer hours, the supervisor notifies the Service Coordinator within 1 business day and documents the notification.
The agency captures every Medicaid visit in EVV and bills only for authorized, verified visits, as described in SVC-07. Billing follows each payer's claim submission rules and deadlines.

For a critical incident involving a CHC Waiver, OBRA Waiver or Act 150 participant, the agency that discovers the incident notifies the participant's Service Coordinator within 24 hours of discovery. The agency also submits the first section of the critical incident report within 48 hours, as described in SAF-02 and the OLTL bulletin.

The agency treats its staff as mandatory reporters under the Adult Protective Services Act and the Older Adults Protective Services Act, as described in the OLTL bulletin, and follows SAF-01 for suspected abuse, neglect and exploitation.

The Administrator logs each Medicaid critical incident with the date and time discovered, the date and time the Service Coordinator was notified, the date the first section was submitted and any follow-up the MCO or OLTL requests.

The agency participates in MCO and OLTL care coordination, such as case conferences, care plan reviews, audits and quality reviews, and provides requested records within the time requested, consistent with privacy rules (see CR-03).
The Administrator tracks MCO and OLTL bulletins, provider manuals and contract updates, reviews them at least quarterly, and updates agency policies when a payer requirement changes (see GOV-03).
Billing staff reconcile Medicaid payments and denials monthly, correct claim errors promptly and refund overpayments in accordance with the corporate compliance policy (see GOV-05).

When serving a participant who has both Medicaid and private-pay hours, the agency keeps the services, schedules and billing separate. It does not bill Medicaid for private-pay hours or require private payment for authorized Medicaid services (see CR-06).
The Administrator reviews payer coordination, critical incident timeliness and claim accuracy at least quarterly in the quality assurance program (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Manages OLTL enrollment and MCO credentialing, confirms network status and rates in writing, ensures critical incident notice and reports are timely and keeps payer requirements current.
Verify eligibility, program, authorization and Service Coordinator information before accepting Medicaid referrals.
Provides services consistent with the participant's plan and authorization, and notifies the Service Coordinator of changes and incidents.
Submit accurate claims for authorized, EVV-verified visits and reconcile payments.

documentation: OLTL enrollment correspondence and application records
Payer file with each CHC-MCO's credentialing, contracting and rate information (including W1793 rate) and the date and source of each answer
Written confirmation of network status, when received
Referral, eligibility and authorization records
Notifications to the Service Coordinator about changes
Critical incident log showing date and time of discovery, 24-hour Service Coordinator notice and 48-hour report submission
Claim, payment and denial reconciliation records
Review of MCO and OLTL bulletins and policy updates

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] employees, caregivers, office staff, contractors, the Administrator and governing body members
policies.purpose: To protect clients from abuse, neglect, exploitation and abandonment. To make sure every suspicion is reported to the correct Pennsylvania authority without delay, and that no one who reports in good faith is punished.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, exploitation or abandonment of any client. All staff are mandatory reporters. Anyone who has reasonable cause to suspect that a client has been abused, neglected, exploited or abandoned must report it immediately, whoever the suspected person is (staff, family, another person or the client). Under the Older Adults Protective Services Act (35 P.S. §10225.701), an employee or administrator with reasonable cause to suspect abuse of a recipient age 60 or older must immediately make an oral report to the Area Agency on Aging. Under the Adult Protective Services Act (Act 70 of 2010), suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation or abandonment of an adult age 18-59 with a disability is reported to the statewide line, 1-800-490-8505 (24 hours a day, 7 days a week). A call to the Department of Human Services about one of the four serious allegations does not satisfy the hotline report; the hotline call must still be made. For CHC and OBRA Waiver participants, the agency also follows the OLTL abuse and critical incident provisions (55 Pa. Code §52.16) and reports under SAF-02. Reporting abuse and neglect is a required competency topic for every direct care worker under 28 Pa. Code §611.55(b). Staff may not delay a report to consult a supervisor, and the agency will never retaliate against a reporter. Suspected abuse of a child is reported under the Child Protective Services Law (ChildLine, 1-800-932-0313), and staff must call 911 when someone is in immediate danger.

definitions.definition: Willful infliction of injury, unreasonable confinement, intimidation, punishment, or sexual abuse that results in physical harm, pain or mental anguish, or the willful deprivation of goods or services necessary to maintain physical or mental health. The definitions in the OAPSA, the APS Act and 55 Pa. Code §52.16 control.
Failure to provide the care, goods or services needed to maintain a client's health and safety. This includes a caregiver's failure to show up for scheduled care that leaves a client at risk.
Improper use of a client's money, property or resources for another person's benefit. Examples are taking cash, borrowing money, using a client's cards or accepting large gifts.
Desertion of a client by a person who has assumed responsibility for the client's care, leaving the client without necessary support.
A good-faith belief based on what a person sees, hears or is told. Proof is not required, and investigating is not the reporter's job.
A person required by law to report suspected abuse. For this agency, every employee and administrator is one.
The county-level protective services agency that receives oral reports about clients age 60 and older.

procedures: The Administrator posts, in the office and in the caregiver app or handbook, the current AAA protective services number for each county served ([LOCAL AAA PROTECTIVE SERVICES PHONE]), the AAA after-hours line ([AAA 24-HOUR PHONE]), the statewide hotline 1-800-490-8505, and ChildLine 1-800-932-0313.

At hire and before first client contact, every worker receives training on recognizing and reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation as part of the competency content under 28 Pa. Code §611.55(b) (see CMP-02). The worker signs an acknowledgment that they are a mandatory reporter. Training is repeated at least annually (PER-02).
Staff are encouraged to complete the free online mandated-reporter training offered by DHS. The Administrator keeps the certificates in the personnel record.

A worker who sees, hears or suspects abuse, neglect, exploitation or abandonment ensures the client's immediate safety first. If the client is in immediate danger or needs emergency care, the worker calls 911.

The worker then reports immediately and personally. For a client age 60 or older, the worker makes an oral report to the AAA protective services line. For a client age 18-59 with a disability, the worker calls 1-800-490-8505. If the client's age or status is unclear, the worker calls the hotline. The worker may not wait for a supervisor's approval, and the worker's own report cannot be delegated.

For the four serious allegations under the APS Act, the worker or Administrator also notifies law enforcement, and still makes the hotline report. A call to DHS about one of those allegations does not replace the hotline call.

The worker notifies the Administrator or on-call supervisor ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]) as soon as the report has been made, and in any event the same day. If the Administrator is the suspected person, the worker reports directly to the authorities and to the governing body ([GOVERNING BODY CONTACT]).

The worker records the facts in an incident report the same day: who, what, when, where, observations in the worker's own words, the client's statements quoted, who was called, the time of each call and any report or reference number given. The worker does not interview the client in a leading way, does not confront the suspected person and does not alter the scene or evidence.

The Administrator confirms within 1 business day that the oral report was made. If it was not, the Administrator makes it at once. The agency never treats an internal report as a substitute for the required external report.

For CHC, OBRA Waiver or Act 150 participants, the Administrator also completes the critical incident reporting steps in SAF-02 (Service Coordinator notice within 24 hours; first section of the report within 48 hours), even if the participant declines.

The Administrator removes a staff member suspected of abuse from contact with the client, or places the worker on leave pending the investigation, as appropriate to protect the client. The Administrator does not take a worker off the schedule in a way that tips off the suspect before authorities have been called, if law enforcement asks the agency to wait.
The agency cooperates fully with the AAA, DHS, the Department of Health, law enforcement and the CHC-MCO. The Administrator provides records on request, subject to the law (CR-03).
The Administrator reviews each substantiated or credible allegation within 10 business days, identifies contributing factors and updates the service plan, supervision or training as needed (GOV-04).

Retaliation against any person who reports in good faith, including reduced hours, discipline, threats or discharge, is prohibited. Any retaliation is itself grounds for termination. A worker who believes they were retaliated against reports to the Administrator or the governing body.

Prevention measures include the pre-hire screening in HIR-01 and HIR-02, supervisory visits (SVC-04), professional boundaries (PER-05), property and gift rules (CR-04) and the prohibition on power of attorney and guardianship (CP-03).
The Administrator provides each client a plain-language statement of the right to be free from abuse, with the hotline numbers, in the consumer information packet (CP-05, CR-01).
The Administrator reviews all abuse reports quarterly with the governing body in aggregate form to identify patterns.

responsibilities.duty: Report suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation or abandonment immediately to the correct authority. Notify the Administrator. Document the facts. Never retaliate.
Posts reporting numbers, trains staff, verifies that external reports were made, completes critical incident reports (SAF-02), protects clients and reporters, and reviews each case.
Watch for signs of abuse during visits, take reports from staff and clients, and make sure external reports are not delayed.
Receives reports about the Administrator and reviews aggregate data.

documentation: Signed mandatory-reporter acknowledgment and training records for each worker
Incident report for each suspected event, with call times and report reference numbers
Copies of any written follow-up to AAA, DHS or law enforcement
Critical incident report copies for CHC/OBRA participants (SAF-02)
Administrator's case review notes and corrective actions
Quarterly aggregate summary presented to the governing body

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] staff, the Administrator and the governing body; all clients, including CHC, OBRA Waiver, Act 150 and private-pay clients
policies.purpose: To make sure incidents involving clients or the agency are reported, investigated, managed and reduced. This includes critical incidents under the OLTL rules, events the Department of Health requires under 28 Pa. Code §51.3, and any case of serious noncompliance.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has written procedures for preventing, reporting, notifying about, investigating and managing incidents, as 55 Pa. Code §52.17(b)-(f) requires of OLTL home and community-based services providers. For CHC, OBRA Waiver and Act 150 participants, the agency that discovers a critical incident (as defined in 55 Pa. Code §52.3 and clarified by the OLTL Critical Incident Management Bulletin of Feb. 23, 2023) submits the first section of the incident report on the Department's form within 48 hours of discovery. The agency informs the participant's Service Coordinator within 24 hours of discovery. Under the Community HealthChoices Agreement (Exhibit W(1)), network providers report to the CHC-MCO, which uses the Enterprise Incident Management (EIM) system. The agency reports even if the participant declines. Failure to report can bring sanctions up to termination of the provider contract. Separately, the agency reports events listed in 28 Pa. Code §51.3 to the Department of Health: deaths under unusual circumstances, death or serious injury from a medication error, transfer to a hospital because of injury or accident, abuse complaints, rape, disaster-related disruption of services, loss of vital utilities and unlicensed practice. The agency also notifies the Department of Health in writing, immediately, if it knows it is out of compliance in a way that seriously compromises quality assurance or client safety, giving the reason and the corrective steps (§51.3(e)). Staff are trained on critical incident reporting (55 Pa. Code §52.21). Incident reporting never replaces the separate duty to report abuse under SAF-01.

definitions.definition: An event defined in 55 Pa. Code §52.3 and the OLTL Critical Incident Management Bulletin that involves a participant and must be reported to OLTL's systems. It includes, at a minimum, deaths, serious injuries and hospitalizations, abuse, neglect, exploitation or abandonment, and missing persons. The Administrator keeps the current bulletin on file and trains from it.
An event the Department of Health requires a licensed provider to report, listed in the policy statement above.
The CHC-MCO or Waiver Service Coordinator assigned to the participant.
The Department of Human Services' electronic incident management system, used by CHC-MCOs and providers for critical incident reports.
The moment any agency employee first learns of the incident. Time limits start at that moment, not when the Administrator is told.
A known failure to meet a licensing requirement that seriously compromises quality assurance or client safety.

procedures: Any employee who discovers or is told of an incident makes the client safe, calls 911 if needed, and notifies the Administrator or on-call supervisor ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]) immediately. The employee must not wait until the end of a shift.
The employee completes the agency incident form the same day, covering the date, time, place, persons involved, what happened, injuries, actions taken, persons notified and witnesses.

Within 1 hour of being notified, or as soon as practical, the Administrator decides whether the event is (a) a critical incident for a CHC, OBRA Waiver or Act 150 participant, (b) a §51.3 reportable event, (c) a suspected abuse case requiring the SAF-01 report, or any combination. When unsure, the Administrator reports.
For a critical incident, the Administrator notifies the participant's Service Coordinator within 24 hours of discovery and documents the name of the person told, the date and the time.

For a critical incident, the Administrator submits the first section of the incident report within 48 hours of discovery, through the CHC-MCO's EIM process or as directed by OLTL for OBRA Waiver and Act 150 participants. The agency reports even if the participant declines, and records that the participant declined.
The Administrator provides follow-up and final information on the incident when the MCO, OLTL or the Service Coordinator requests it, and records the date and content of each submission.

For a §51.3 reportable event, the Administrator notifies the Department of Health, Division of Home Health, in writing as soon as possible, and no later than the timeframe stated in 28 Pa. Code §51.3. The Administrator verifies the current timeframe in the full text and records it on the agency reporting chart. The report states what happened, the client's status and the action taken.

If the event involves a medication error causing death or serious injury, a hospital transfer from an injury or accident, rape, loss of vital utilities or disruption from a disaster, the Administrator reports it under §51.3 whether or not the client is a Medicaid participant.

If the Administrator learns that the agency is out of compliance in a way that seriously compromises quality assurance or client safety, the Administrator notifies the Department of Health in writing immediately, stating the reason and the corrective steps. The Administrator informs the governing body the same day.
The Administrator notifies the client's representative and family contact as the client permits and as the law requires, unless the family member is a suspect.

The Administrator begins an internal investigation within 1 business day. This includes interviews, a review of schedules and documentation, and a review of the service plan, and is completed within 10 business days unless an outside investigation requires the agency to wait.

The Administrator reviews each incident to decide whether it was preventable. Where it was, the Administrator documents corrective action such as retraining, a service plan revision, more supervision, equipment or a discipline decision (PER-05).
Within 7 days of an incident, the Administrator updates the service plan if needed (SVC-03) and informs the supervisor and affected caregivers.

Incident reporting training is part of orientation and annual training for every employee, covering what counts as an incident, the 24-hour and 48-hour limits and how to complete the form (PER-02; 55 Pa. Code §52.21). The Administrator keeps sign-in sheets.
The Administrator logs every incident in a central incident log and reviews it quarterly with the governing body for trends and to find ways to reduce preventable incidents (GOV-04).
No staff member is disciplined for making a good-faith report. Failure to report an incident is a disciplinary matter.

responsibilities.duty: Make the client safe, notify the Administrator immediately and complete the incident form the same day.
Classifies the incident, meets the 24-hour Service Coordinator notice and 48-hour critical incident report deadlines, makes Department of Health reports, investigates, and keeps the log.
Take reports after hours, secure records and help with follow-up.
Receives notice of serious noncompliance and reviews incident trends and prevention.

documentation: Agency incident form for every event
Copy of each critical incident report submitted, with the date and time of first-section submission and of follow-up
Record of the 24-hour Service Coordinator notification (name, date and time)
Copies of §51.3 notices to the Department of Health and any responses
Written notice of serious noncompliance under §51.3(e), if made
Investigation notes, findings and corrective actions
Central incident log and quarterly review minutes
Training sign-in sheets for incident reporting

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All direct care workers, supervisors and office staff with consumer contact; all clients
policies.purpose: To reduce the spread of infection among clients and staff by requiring training, hand hygiene, appropriate use of personal protective equipment, tuberculosis screening and exposure response.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires every direct care worker to be competent in basic infection control and universal precautions before being assigned to or referred to any client, as 28 Pa. Code §611.55(b) requires. Each direct care worker, and each office staff member or contractor with direct consumer contact, must document tuberculosis screening and freedom from active TB before consumer contact. Screening follows CDC guidelines and may not be more than 1 year before the start date (28 Pa. Code §611.56(a); see HS-01). A worker with TB symptoms or a known TB exposure does not have consumer contact until medically cleared. The agency maintains an exposure control plan consistent with the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, and supplies workers with personal protective equipment and hand-hygiene supplies at no cost to the worker. The Administrator confirms the OSHA exposure control plan requirements before adoption, since they were not among the sources reviewed for this manual.

definitions.definition: Treating the blood and certain body fluids of every person as potentially infectious and using barriers such as gloves and eye protection accordingly.
Gloves, masks, gowns, eye protection and similar items used to protect the worker or client from contact with infectious materials.
Contact with blood or other potentially infectious material through a needlestick, cut, splash to the eyes, nose or mouth, or on broken skin.
The agency's written plan identifying tasks with exposure risk, protective measures, training, and the response to exposures.

procedures: Before any client assignment or referral, the Administrator verifies and documents that the worker has completed competency training or an exam covering infection control and universal precautions (CMP-01, CMP-02).

Before any consumer contact, the Administrator verifies and files the worker's TB screening and the documentation of freedom from active TB, dated not more than 1 year before the start date (HS-01). The worker is not scheduled until the file is complete.

The Administrator writes and keeps current an exposure control plan that identifies tasks with exposure risk (such as personal care, wound-adjacent care, handling soiled linens and sharps), the protective measures for each, and the exposure response steps. The Administrator reviews it at least annually and whenever tasks change.

The agency provides, at no cost, a PPE kit for every caregiver: disposable gloves in multiple sizes, masks, hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol, disposable aprons or gowns where needed, eye protection and a biohazard bag. Supervisors check supply levels at each supervisory visit and the office restocks within 2 business days of a request.

Training in orientation and annually covers hand hygiene (before and after each client contact, after glove removal and after toileting or handling soiled items), correct donning and removal of PPE, cleaning of surfaces and equipment, laundry handling, sharps safety, respiratory etiquette and when to stay home.

Workers wash hands with soap and water, or use alcohol-based sanitizer when hands are not visibly soiled, before and after every client contact and between tasks. They use gloves for any contact with blood, body fluids, broken skin or soiled items.

Workers do not recap, bend or carry loose sharps. Workers do not perform tasks that involve injections or sharps unless permitted under SVC-01. If a sharp is found in the home, the worker does not handle it and reports it to the Administrator.

A worker who has a fever, vomiting, diarrhea, a draining rash or other contagious symptoms, or who has TB symptoms (cough lasting 3 weeks or more, night sweats, unexplained weight loss or bloody sputum), calls the office before the shift. The scheduler arranges coverage, and the worker returns only when symptom-free or medically cleared. A worker with TB symptoms or exposure does not return until cleared by a healthcare provider, and the clearance is filed.

If a client has a known or suspected infectious illness, the worker follows the client's care plan and the precautions the client's clinician orders. The Administrator informs assigned workers of any precautions needed, sharing only what is necessary (CR-03).

After an exposure incident, the worker washes the area immediately, reports to the Administrator at once, and is directed to medical evaluation as soon as possible. The Administrator completes an incident report the same day and applies SAF-02 if reporting is required.
The Administrator reviews every exposure incident and reports of client infections linked to care to find causes and corrective action (GOV-04).
The agency posts or provides a one-page hand-hygiene and PPE guide in the caregiver handbook and app.
During supervisory visits (SVC-04), the supervisor observes infection control practices and documents corrections and retraining.

responsibilities.duty: Complete training, use universal precautions and PPE, practice hand hygiene, stay home when ill and report exposures at once.
Maintains the exposure control plan, verifies TB screening and competency, supplies PPE and reviews exposure incidents.
Observe practice, check PPE supplies and retrain as needed.
Arranges coverage when a worker is excluded for illness or exposure.

documentation: Competency exam or training record covering infection control and universal precautions
TB screening results and freedom-from-active-TB documentation, dated within 1 year before start
Return-to-work clearance after TB symptoms or exposure
Written exposure control plan and annual review record
PPE issuance and supply logs
Training sign-in sheets (orientation and annual)
Exposure incident reports and follow-up
Supervisory visit observations of infection control

policies.title: Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] staff and all clients
policies.purpose: To make sure clients continue to receive needed care, or are safely referred, during emergencies, severe weather, utility loss, public health events and other disasters, and that required reports are made.
policies.policy: Chapter 611 of Title 28 of the Pa. Code has no separate emergency preparedness section, so this policy is [AGENCY NAME]'s own design. The agency maintains a written emergency and disaster plan that ranks clients by risk, keeps current emergency contacts, sets a call-tree for staff and clients, and defines how the agency continues or transfers services. Disruption of services due to a disaster and loss of vital utilities are reportable events under 28 Pa. Code §51.3 (see SAF-02). The agency tests its call-tree at least annually and reviews the plan at least annually.

definitions.definition: An event such as severe weather, flood, fire, power or heat or water loss, pandemic, public safety event or other incident that disrupts the agency's ability to deliver care or threatens client safety.
Classifying each client as high, medium or low priority according to dependence on caregivers and on electricity-dependent equipment, mobility and cognition.
A written list showing who calls whom, in what order, to reach staff and clients during an emergency.

procedures: At intake, the supervisor completes an emergency information sheet with the client: emergency contacts, physician, pharmacy, known medical conditions, medicines list, allergies, equipment that needs power (oxygen concentrator, hospital bed, lift), mobility limits, pets, preferred hospital and evacuation help available.

The supervisor assigns each client a risk rank (high, medium or low). A client who cannot self-evacuate, uses electrical life-support equipment, has cognitive impairment or has no other caregiver is high-risk. The Administrator keeps a master list sorted by rank and updates it when conditions change or at least every 6 months.
The Administrator maintains the staff call-tree with after-hours numbers and backups for each person. The call-tree is kept in the office and as a secure electronic copy off-site.

The Administrator keeps a list of local emergency contacts: [LOCAL EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT AGENCY PHONE], [AREA AGENCY ON AGING PHONE], utility companies, and for Medicaid participants, the Service Coordinator for each. The list is reviewed every 6 months.

When an emergency is forecast or begins, the Administrator or designee activates the plan, calls high-risk clients first, confirms their safety and plans for the next 72 hours, and tells staff which visits will go forward.
Caregivers on shift when an emergency occurs stay with the client, call 911 if needed, help the client follow the client's own plan and notify the office as soon as it is safe.

If a caregiver cannot reach a client due to conditions, the caregiver calls the office. The office calls the client or emergency contact, and if the client may be in danger, asks local emergency services to do a welfare check.
If the agency cannot staff a visit, the scheduler uses backup caregivers, then asks the client's family or Service Coordinator for help, and documents the missed visit and notices (SVC-06).
Workers are never required to put themselves in danger to reach a client. A worker who judges travel unsafe calls the office and the office decides on alternatives (SAF-05).
The Administrator informs the Service Coordinator of Medicaid participants when a high-risk client's services are disrupted, and determines whether the event is a critical incident under SAF-02.
The Administrator reports to the Department of Health under 28 Pa. Code §51.3 any disaster that disrupts services and any loss of vital utilities, and records the report.
After the emergency, the Administrator confirms the welfare of every client, restores services, completes a written after-action review within 14 days and updates the plan.

Each year the Administrator tests the call-tree by calling a sample of staff and high-risk clients, records response times and fixes gaps. Staff are trained on the plan at orientation and annually (PER-02).

Each client receives, in the information packet, a written note on what to expect from the agency in an emergency and what the client should do, including keeping a bag of medicines and papers ready (CP-04).

responsibilities.duty: Owns the plan, maintains the risk-ranked list and call-tree, activates the plan, reports to the Department of Health and reviews after events.
Collect emergency information at intake and assign risk ranks. Contact clients during an event.
Arranges coverage and logs disrupted visits.
Protect the client, call 911 when needed and report to the office.

documentation: Written emergency and disaster plan with annual review date
Client emergency information sheets and risk ranking list
Staff call-tree and emergency contact list
Annual call-tree test results
Event log, contacts made and missed visits during an emergency
§51.3 notices to the Department of Health where applicable
After-action review report
Training records on the emergency plan

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All direct care workers, supervisors and office staff; all clients and household members
policies.purpose: To protect caregivers from injury, exposure, violence and unsafe conditions while working in clients' homes and in the agency office, and to set clear steps for leaving an unsafe setting.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is committed to a safe workplace for caregivers, including the client's home. Chapter 611 recognizes that an agency may limit accommodations or give shorter termination notice where a worker's health, safety or welfare is at risk (28 Pa. Code §611.57(a); see CP-01 and CP-02). Workers may leave an unsafe setting and report it, without penalty. The agency performs a home safety check at intake, trains workers on safe transfers and difficult behaviors (the competency topic in 28 Pa. Code §611.55(b)), and applies the bloodborne pathogen protections in 29 CFR 1910.1030 (see SAF-03). No worker, including a provisionally hired worker, is assigned to a client until competency has been established, including difficult behaviors and safe handling (28 Pa. Code §611.54(a) requires competency first; see PRV-01 and PRV-02). Workers, and anyone affiliated with the agency, must never assume power of attorney or guardianship over a client or require a client to endorse checks to the agency (28 Pa. Code §611.57(b); see CP-03), because such arrangements create conflict and danger in the working relationship.

definitions.definition: Any act or threat of physical violence, harassment, intimidation, or other threatening behavior directed at a worker, including by a client, household member or visitor, or by a coworker.
A home or situation where the worker reasonably believes there is a risk of injury, violence, harassment, serious infection, hazardous conditions or illegal activity.
A structured review of the home done at intake, covering hazards such as trip hazards, pets, smoke detectors, firearms, lighting, utilities, safe parking and equipment.
Client behaviors such as aggression, confusion, refusal of care, wandering or inappropriate remarks, which workers must be trained to manage.

procedures: At intake, the supervisor completes a home safety checklist during the assessment visit (SVC-02). It covers entry and parking safety, lighting, stairs and trip hazards, working smoke detectors, pets and their control, presence of firearms (which should be stored locked and unloaded), smoking, pest or mold problems, utilities, equipment condition and any known history of aggression by the client or others in the home.

The supervisor records hazards, discusses them with the client, and writes agreed fixes into the service plan (SVC-03). If hazards cannot be reduced to a safe level, the Administrator decides whether to limit tasks, change the plan, adjust the schedule or decline or end services under CP-02, using the safety exception in §611.57(a) when appropriate.
The agency shares with the assigned worker, before the first visit, the home safety findings and any known risk of difficult behavior, limited to what the worker needs to know (CR-03).

At orientation and annually, every worker is trained in body mechanics and safe transfers, recognizing and de-escalating difficult behaviors, personal safety (situational awareness, exit routes, safe parking), infection control (SAF-03) and how to report threats or injuries (PER-02). The Administrator does not assign a worker to clients with transfer or behavioral needs until training and a competency check have been documented (CMP-01 to CMP-04).
A provisional hire is not placed with any client until competency is documented and supervised observation is in place (PRV-01, PRV-02).
Workers do not lift or transfer beyond their training or the client's care plan. If a transfer is unsafe without equipment or a second person, the worker stops and calls the supervisor.

A worker may leave any setting that feels unsafe. The worker must (a) remove themselves from danger first, calling 911 if needed, (b) call the on-call supervisor ([ON-CALL PHONE]) as soon as safe, and (c) complete an incident report by the end of the shift. The agency will not discipline a worker for leaving in good faith.

When a worker leaves, the supervisor ensures the client is safe, which may mean calling the client's emergency contact, the Service Coordinator, or requesting a welfare check. The supervisor documents the client contact and follows SVC-06 on missed visits.

The supervisor contacts the worker within 24 hours of any threat or violent event to offer support, reviews the circumstances and decides on service changes. Incidents are logged, and incidents requiring reporting are handled under SAF-02.
Workers do not enter a home where a person appears impaired or threatening, and do not remain if firearms are displayed in a threatening way or illegal activity occurs.

Sexual harassment, verbal abuse or discrimination by a client or household member is not tolerated. The agency will address it with the client, adjust assignments, may limit or end services in accordance with CP-02 and will support the worker. Workers who report are protected from retaliation.
Workers may not take on legal or financial roles for clients: no power of attorney, guardianship or check endorsement (CP-03, CR-04). A worker who is asked to do so declines and tells the supervisor.
Workers report injuries at work immediately. The Administrator arranges medical care, completes the incident report and workers' compensation notice as required (PER-04, PER-03).
Office safety: the office has a visitor policy, locked access to client records, an emergency exit plan and an alert procedure for threatening visitors or callers.
The Administrator reviews all worker safety incidents quarterly and uses them to improve screening, training and assignments (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Follow safe practices, use PPE, stop unsafe tasks, leave unsafe settings and report incidents promptly.
Perform home safety checks, brief workers, support workers after incidents and arrange alternative services.
Trains staff, decides on service limits or termination for safety reasons, reviews incidents and makes sure workers are not retaliated against.
Respond to worker safety calls at any hour.

documentation: Completed home safety checklist for each client
Service plan notes on safety hazards and agreed fixes
Training records on safe transfers, difficult behaviors and personal safety
Incident reports for threats, violence, unsafe-setting departures and worker injuries
Supervisor follow-up notes with workers and clients
Quarterly review of worker safety incidents
Records of any service limits or termination for safety reasons (CP-02)

policies.title: Transporting Clients
policies.applies_to: All direct care workers who drive clients or use a vehicle on agency business; the Administrator and scheduling staff
policies.purpose: To set safe, authorized and insured rules for any transportation of clients, and to make sure crashes are reported and managed.
policies.policy: Chapter 611 of Title 28 of the Pa. Code sets no rule on transporting clients, so this policy is [AGENCY NAME]'s own design. Workers may transport a client only if the client's service plan authorizes it, the worker holds a valid driver's license, the vehicle is registered, inspected and insured, and the agency carries hired and non-owned auto coverage. Any crash or injury during transport is reported as an incident under SAF-02. Workers who are not authorized or do not meet these conditions may not drive clients.

definitions.definition: Driving a client in a vehicle, whether the worker's or the client's, as part of the services in the service plan, such as to medical appointments, shopping or errands.
Liability insurance that covers the agency when workers use personal or rented vehicles on agency business.
A worker approved in writing by the Administrator after the license, driving record and insurance checks in this policy.

procedures: The Administrator keeps current hired and non-owned auto liability coverage in place with limits set by the governing body, and files the policy in the office ([INSURANCE CARRIER], [POLICY NUMBER]).

Transportation is provided only when the service plan, agreed with the client, lists it (SVC-03). Without that, workers decline politely and tell the supervisor. The plan states the purposes of trips, whose vehicle is used and any limits.

Before authorizing a worker to drive clients, the Administrator verifies a valid Pennsylvania (or other valid state) driver's license, reviews the driving record at hire and annually, and records the worker's vehicle registration, current inspection and proof of auto insurance meeting Pennsylvania minimums. The worker gives updated proof at every renewal.

The Administrator excludes from driving any worker with a suspended license, a serious or recent driving violation (such as DUI) or lapsed insurance. The Administrator documents the decision, and the worker may still do non-driving duties.
The Administrator gives the worker written approval to drive clients only after the above checks. Workers sign a transportation acknowledgment covering the rules below.

Rules for the trip: everyone wears a seat belt; the worker does not use a handheld phone, text, or drive while impaired, drowsy or in unsafe weather; the vehicle is clean and in working order; and the client sits in a safe position. A child restraint is used where a child passenger is allowed.
The worker does not transport anyone other than the client, nor make personal stops, unless the service plan permits.

Workers help clients enter and exit the vehicle safely using safe transfer techniques they have been trained on (SAF-05). Workers do not lift clients beyond their training. A client who uses a wheelchair requiring a ramp or lift is transported only in a vehicle designed for it, or the worker arranges alternate transport.

Workers do not accept payment for gas or mileage from clients, and do not borrow or use a client's vehicle, unless the service plan and Administrator specifically authorize the use and the client's insurance and agency coverage permit it. Any mileage billing follows the service agreement (CR-06).
Time spent driving a client is recorded as work time through EVV or timekeeping (SVC-07, PER-04), and mileage reimbursement for workers follows the agency pay policy (PER-04).
If the worker's license or insurance lapses, the worker tells the Administrator at once and stops driving clients until the issue is fixed.

If a crash occurs, the worker calls 911 if anyone is hurt, ensures the client's safety, exchanges information as required by law, and calls the on-call supervisor immediately ([ON-CALL PHONE]). The worker completes an incident report by the end of the shift.

The Administrator reports the crash under SAF-02, including a critical incident report and Service Coordinator notice within 24 hours where the client is a CHC, OBRA Waiver or Act 150 participant, and a Department of Health report if a hospital transfer from injury or accident occurs. The Administrator notifies the insurer, the client's representative and, as appropriate, the Service Coordinator.
The Administrator reviews every crash and near-miss, decides on corrective action and may suspend driving authorization.
Annually, the Administrator reviews the list of authorized drivers, license status, insurance proofs and incident history.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains insurance, authorizes drivers, checks licenses and records, reviews crashes and files reports.
Confirm that the service plan authorizes transportation and observe safe practice at visits.
Keep license, registration and insurance current, follow safety rules and report incidents immediately.
Assigns transportation visits only to authorized drivers.

documentation: Hired and non-owned auto insurance policy and renewal
Driver authorization form, license copy, driving record review and annual updates
Vehicle registration, inspection and insurance proof for each driver
Signed transportation acknowledgment
Service plan section authorizing transportation
Time and mileage records
Crash and incident reports, insurer notices and review notes
Annual driver list review

policies.title: Caregiver Qualifications and Employment Classification
policies.applies_to: Administrator, hiring and scheduling staff, and all direct care workers
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who gives direct, non-medical care to a consumer for [AGENCY NAME] is qualified under Chapter 611, has demonstrated competency before assignment, and is employed as a W-2 employee of the agency.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] employs its direct care workers as W-2 employees. It does not treat them as independent contractors and does not operate a worker registry. Pennsylvania has no separate state registry or certification for home care aides, so a worker's qualification rests on the hiring, clearance, competency and health screening requirements of 28 Pa. Code Chapter 611. Before hiring, the agency holds a face-to-face interview, obtains at least two satisfactory references, and requires a criminal history report and, where applicable, ChildLine verification (28 Pa. Code §611.51(a)). Before any assignment to a consumer, the worker must hold a Pennsylvania nurse license, pass the agency's competency exam, or complete an approved training program, such as a Medicaid waiver training program or the Pennsylvania Department of Education nurse aide program (28 Pa. Code §611.55(a)). The agency discloses employee status to every consumer in the Consumer Information Packet (CP-05). As a third-party employer, the agency does not rely on the companionship or live-in exemptions removed by 29 CFR 552 (see PER-04). This policy uses the defined terms in 28 Pa. Code §611.5.

definitions.definition: A person who receives home care services from the agency, as defined in 28 Pa. Code §611.5. This manual uses "client" and "consumer" interchangeably.
An employee of the agency who provides services directly to a consumer, as defined in 28 Pa. Code §611.5.
Face-to-face contact with a consumer in the course of providing services, as defined in 28 Pa. Code §611.5.
Socialization, support and help with instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs), as defined in 28 Pa. Code §611.5.
A registered nurse (RN) or licensed practical nurse (LPN) licensed in Pennsylvania, as defined in 28 Pa. Code §611.5.
A worker whom the agency pays through payroll, with tax withholding and an IRS Form W-2 issued each year. The agency controls the worker's schedule, training and supervision.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a written direct care worker job description. It states that the position is a W-2 employee position, lists the duties allowed under SVC-01, and lists the minimum qualifications in this policy.

Hiring staff post job advertisements stating that the position is an employee position with the agency. They do not recruit workers as independent contractors or place workers through a registry model.
Each applicant completes a written application showing work history, the names and contact information of at least two references, and consent for criminal history and ChildLine checks.
The Administrator or designee holds a face-to-face interview with every applicant before hiring and records the interview date and interviewer on the Interview Record (see HIR-01).
Hiring staff obtain at least two satisfactory references: positive, verifiable and from unrelated persons. They record the reference name, date and result on the Reference Record (see HIR-01).

Before any hire offer becomes final, hiring staff obtain the criminal history report and, if the worker will have contact with children, the ChildLine verification, as set out in CBC-01 through CBC-04 and CAC-01. A person with a prohibited conviction is not hired (CBC-02).
Before consumer contact, hiring staff obtain tuberculosis screening documentation under HS-01.

The Administrator confirms that the worker has met competency by one of three routes: a current Pennsylvania nurse license, a passing score on the agency's competency exam (CMP-01 to CMP-03), or a certificate from an approved training program, such as a Medicaid waiver training program or the Pennsylvania Department of Education nurse aide program. A copy of the license, exam record or certificate goes in the worker file (CMP-04).

A worker is not assigned to or referred to any consumer until competency is documented and the pre-hire clearances in HIR-02 are in the file. The only exception is a provisional hire that meets every condition in PRV-01 and PRV-02.
A worker who holds a nurse license is still hired and assigned only as a direct care worker. The worker does not perform skilled nursing tasks for the agency's home care clients and follows SVC-01.

On the first day, the Administrator or designee issues a written offer or employment agreement stating that the worker is a W-2 employee. The worker completes the federal and state employment, tax withholding and work-eligibility forms through the payroll service (see PER-04).
Scheduling staff do not assign a worker to a consumer until the Administrator initials the Qualification Checklist in the worker file as complete.

The Client Intake Coordinator gives each consumer the Consumer Information Packet, which states that the agency's direct care workers are its employees (CP-05). Staff ask the consumer to sign the acknowledgment page.

Each January the Administrator reviews all worker files against this policy. The review covers classification, competency review dates (CMP-04), TB updates (HS-01) and clearances. Any worker found to be misclassified or missing a required item is removed from the schedule until corrected.
The Administrator reviews this policy with an employment attorney at each annual policy review (GOV-03), including any change to the federal rules at 29 CFR 552.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure every worker is a W-2 employee, meets Chapter 611 qualifications before assignment, and has a complete Qualification Checklist.
Interview applicants, check references, collect clearances and record each step in the worker file.
Assign only workers with a signed Qualification Checklist.
Delivers the Consumer Information Packet that discloses employee status.
Gives accurate application information, completes required training or exam, and follows the job description.

documentation: Application, job description and signed offer letter
Interview Record and Reference Records
Competency documentation (exam record, training certificate or nurse license copy)
Qualification Checklist signed by the Administrator
Payroll and W-2 classification records
Consumer acknowledgment of the Consumer Information Packet
Annual file review record

policies.title: Orientation, Competency Evaluation and Annual Training
policies.applies_to: Administrator, trainers, and all direct care workers
policies.purpose: To make sure every direct care worker completes orientation and a competency evaluation covering all required topics before assignment, and receives training and a competency review every year.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] orients every new direct care worker and evaluates competency before the worker is assigned to any consumer. The exam or training covers confidentiality, consumer control, instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs), changes in the consumer, infection control, universal precautions, emergencies, documentation, abuse and neglect reporting, and difficult behaviors (28 Pa. Code §611.55(b)). For workers who provide personal care, it also covers bathing, toileting, transfers, meals and assistance with self-administered medication (28 Pa. Code §611.55(c)). The agency adds HIPAA privacy training (45 CFR 164.530), bloodborne pathogens training (29 CFR 1910.1030), abuse reporting and critical incident reporting. The critical incident reporting topic applies because the agency serves Medicaid consumers under OLTL programs (55 Pa. Code §52.21). The agency reviews each worker's competency at least once a year, and sooner after discipline for a quality-of-care infraction (28 Pa. Code §611.55(e)). Chapter 611 does not set a minimum number of training hours that the agency has verified, so the agency sets its own hours (below) and confirms with the Department of Health whether any minimum applies.

definitions.definition: The agency's introduction of a new worker to its policies, the consumer's service plan, worker duties and limits, reporting duties and safety rules.
A written or skills-based assessment, or an approved training program, that shows the worker can perform the required tasks safely.
A serious event involving a consumer, such as abuse, neglect, exploitation, a death, a serious injury or a missing person, that must be reported under SAF-02 and payer rules.
A documented failure to follow the service plan, agency policy or accepted practice that harms or could harm a consumer.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a written Orientation and Competency Curriculum. It lists every topic required by 28 Pa. Code §611.55(b), plus the personal care topics in §611.55(c) for workers who provide personal care, plus the agency-added topics.

Before the first consumer assignment, the trainer gives orientation on confidentiality, consumer control, IADLs, recognizing and reporting changes in the consumer, infection control and universal precautions, emergencies, documentation, abuse and neglect reporting, and managing difficult behaviors.

For each worker who will provide personal care, the trainer also covers bathing, toileting, transfers, meal preparation and assistance with self-administered medication. The worker demonstrates each skill to the trainer or a nurse (see CMP-03 and SVC-05).
The trainer adds HIPAA privacy and security training (CR-03). It covers what protected health information is, what the worker may share, and how to report a breach.
The trainer adds bloodborne pathogens training that covers exposure risks, standard precautions, personal protective equipment, sharps, cleanup, and what to do after an exposure (SAF-03).

The trainer adds training on recognizing and reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation (SAF-01) and on reporting critical incidents (SAF-02). The worker learns to whom, how fast and in what form to report.

The worker takes the agency competency exam or presents certificate proof from an approved program under CMP-01. The passing score is [PASSING SCORE]. A worker who does not pass receives remedial training and may retake the exam. The Administrator does not assign the worker until a passing result is recorded.
The trainer signs and dates the Orientation Checklist and the competency record. The worker signs to confirm receipt of training. Both go in the worker file (PER-03, CMP-04).

The agency's standard is a minimum of [ORIENTATION HOURS] hours of orientation and competency evaluation before assignment, and [ANNUAL TRAINING HOURS] hours of in-service training each year. The Administrator confirms with the Department of Health, and with each MCO and OLTL contract, whether any required hours or topics apply, and adjusts these standards if so.
At each annual policy review, the Administrator pulls the full topic and hour list in 55 Pa. Code §52.21 for OLTL home and community-based service staff and adds any missing topic to the curriculum.

Every worker completes annual in-service training. It must include a refresher on infection control and bloodborne pathogens, HIPAA, abuse and neglect reporting, critical incident reporting and emergencies. The Administrator tracks due dates by the worker's hire anniversary.

The Administrator or a delegated nurse reviews each worker's competency at least once every 12 months. The review includes a skills check, a review of documentation and supervisory visit notes (SVC-04), and a review of any complaints. The result is signed and filed.

If a worker is disciplined for a quality-of-care infraction, the Administrator schedules an additional competency review within [DAYS] days. The worker is not assigned to the affected tasks until the review is complete and passed.
The Administrator removes from the schedule any worker whose annual training or competency review is overdue by more than [GRACE PERIOD] days, until it is completed.
The Administrator reviews training records quarterly as part of quality assurance (GOV-04) and corrects gaps.

policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: Administrator, office staff, owners, and all direct care workers
policies.purpose: To keep complete, confidential and inspection-ready personnel files for every direct care worker, office staff member and owner, as Chapter 611 requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a personnel file for each direct care worker. Each file documents the interview date and the references, plus the items required for criminal history, ChildLine verification, competency and health screening (28 Pa. Code §611.51(b)). Criminal history reports or letters are kept for direct care workers, office staff and owners and are available for Department of Health inspection (28 Pa. Code §611.52(f)). They are kept confidential and used only to decide whether to hire, roster or retain a person (28 Pa. Code §611.52(g)). ChildLine verification copies are kept in the file of each worker and office staff member, and for owners, and are available for Department inspection (28 Pa. Code §611.53(c)). Tuberculosis documentation is updated at least every 12 months, counted from the last evaluation, and kept in the individual's file (28 Pa. Code §611.56(b)-(c)). Office staff who have direct consumer contact also have TB records. Record retention periods are set in this policy and confirmed against Chapter 51, Chapter 611 and payer contracts.

definitions.definition: The record for each worker showing the interview date, references, criminal history, ChildLine verification (if applicable), competency documentation and TB documentation.
Agency employees who do not provide direct care, such as schedulers, coordinators and administrative personnel.
A person with an ownership interest in the agency. Owners' criminal history and ChildLine records are kept even if the owner does not work as staff.
A record that only authorized staff may see, and that may be used only for the purpose stated in this policy.

procedures: The Administrator opens a personnel file for each person on the day of the interview. Each file is labeled with the person's name and position and is stored in locked or access-controlled storage.

Direct care worker files hold: the application; the interview date and interviewer; at least two reference records; the criminal history report or letter; ChildLine verification where applicable; competency documentation and any nurse license copy; TB documentation; signed training and orientation records; and the signed job description.
For each worker, the Administrator verifies the file against the Personnel File Checklist before the first assignment and initials it. Items missing from the checklist are not accepted as complete.
Office staff files hold the application, interview notes, criminal history report or letter, ChildLine verification where applicable, and TB documentation if the person has direct consumer contact.
For each owner, the Administrator keeps the criminal history report or letter and the ChildLine verification in a separate Owners' File, stored under the same access controls.

Criminal history records are filed in a separate confidential section of each file. Only the Administrator and the designated hiring staff may open them. Staff use them only to hire, roster or retain, and do not copy or share them for any other purpose (see CBC-03).
ChildLine verification copies are filed in each worker's and office staff member's file and in the Owners' File, in a place where they can be produced on request to Department of Health inspectors.

The Administrator tracks TB documentation by the date of the last evaluation. A new TB record is due no later than 12 months after that date, and the worker is told 30 days in advance (HS-01). The new record is filed and the old record is kept.
The Administrator checks competency documentation and the annual review date in each file (CMP-04). A completed annual review is filed with the date and the reviewer's signature.

Records of discipline, evaluations, supervisory visit results and training are filed in the personnel file or an adjacent section. Records of discipline for quality-of-care infractions are marked for an extra competency review under PER-05.
Medical and health records, including TB results, are kept in a separate section of the file from performance records.

When a worker leaves, the Administrator records the separation date and keeps the file. If a worker returns after a break of 12 months or less, the earlier competency documentation may be used (CMP-04). The agency still obtains a current criminal history check and TB update before reassignment as policy requires.

The agency retains each personnel file for at least seven years after the person's separation, or any longer period required by Chapter 51, Chapter 611, a payer contract or other law. The Administrator confirms the required periods with the Department of Health and with each OLTL or MCO contract, and extends this standard if a longer period applies.
The Administrator limits access to files to the Administrator, designated hiring staff, and Department of Health or payer reviewers. Staff keep a log of who views each file and when.
When a file is destroyed after the retention period, the Administrator authorizes shredding or secure electronic deletion and records the date and method.
Each quarter the Administrator audits a sample of files against the checklist. The results go to the quality assurance review (GOV-04), and any gaps are corrected within 14 days.

responsibilities.duty: Keeps all personnel files complete, controls access, confirms retention periods and audits files.
Collect and file required items and keep criminal history and ChildLine records confidential.
Provide accurate documents and updated TB documentation by the due date.
Provide criminal history reports and ChildLine verification for the Owners' File.

policies.title: Wage, Hour and Overtime Compliance
policies.applies_to: Administrator, payroll staff, scheduling staff and all employees
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] pays every employee at least the minimum wage, pays overtime when due, and pays for all hours worked, including travel between clients and training time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] pays every employee at least the Pennsylvania minimum wage, which is $7.25 per hour in 2026, and pays more when the federal or state rate rises or when the agency sets a higher rate. The agency is a third-party employer of its home care workers. It does not rely on the companionship or live-in exemptions that federal rule 29 CFR 552 removed for third-party employers, and it pays overtime to home care workers when the Fair Labor Standards Act or the Pennsylvania Minimum Wage Act requires it. The agency pays for all hours worked, including time spent traveling between clients during the workday, orientation, training and required meetings. The agency uses a payroll service and reviews this policy with an employment attorney. The Administrator confirms with that attorney the current overtime and travel-time rules before relying on any assumption in this policy.

definitions.definition: All time an employee is required or allowed to work, including time with the client, travel between clients, training and required meetings.
An agency or other business that employs a home care worker, as opposed to the consumer or the consumer's family employing the worker directly.
Pay at one and one-half times the regular rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek, unless an exemption applies.
A fixed, recurring period of seven days, set by the agency as [WORKWEEK START DAY AND TIME].

procedures: The Administrator sets and posts the agency workweek and payday schedule and tells every employee in writing at hire.
At hire, each worker receives a written offer letter stating the hourly rate. The rate is never below the current Pennsylvania minimum wage of $7.25 per hour (2026).

The Administrator reviews the minimum wage rate each January and whenever a law changes, including any increase passed by the Pennsylvania General Assembly. Any increase takes effect on the legal effective date.

The agency pays all workers hourly. Hours are taken from Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) records and time records under SVC-07. The agency does not pay a flat amount per visit that could fall below the minimum wage for hours worked.

The agency treats time spent traveling between one client's home and another during the workday as paid work time. The Administrator confirms the rules for the first and last trips of the day with the employment attorney and records the written rule in the Payroll Procedure.
Orientation, competency evaluation, required annual training, staff meetings and supervisory visits are paid time. Workers record this time on their timesheets.

Payroll staff add together all hours worked for the agency in the workweek across all clients and activities. For hours over 40 they pay overtime at one and one-half times the regular rate, as required by the FLSA and the Pennsylvania Minimum Wage Act.

The agency does not use a live-in or companionship exemption to avoid overtime for third-party employed workers (29 CFR 552). If a client's needs involve overnight stays, the Administrator reviews pay with the employment attorney before scheduling.

Scheduling staff check weekly totals before scheduling overtime hours. They get approval from the Administrator before any worker is scheduled for more than 40 hours. Payers are told about authorized-hours and rate limits through SVC-09.
Workers may not work off the clock. A supervisor who learns of unrecorded work must report it to payroll the same day so it is paid.
Workers report any error in their pay to the Administrator in writing. The Administrator investigates within 5 business days and corrects any underpayment on the next payroll.

Payroll staff keep time and pay records for each employee, including hours worked per day and per workweek, rate of pay, gross wages, deductions and dates paid. Records are retained for the longest period required by federal or state wage and hour law, and no less than three years.
The agency registers with the Pennsylvania Department of Labor & Industry as an employer for unemployment compensation tax and withholds and reports taxes through its payroll service.

The Administrator meets with the payroll service and an employment attorney each year and whenever a law changes, to review classification, overtime, travel time and training pay, and to update this policy (GOV-03).
The agency does not retaliate against any employee who asks about or complains about pay.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure pay practices comply with law, reviews rates every January, and consults the employment attorney.
Calculate hours, minimum wage and overtime accurately and keep pay records.
Monitor weekly hours and obtain approval before scheduling overtime.
Record all hours worked accurately and report pay errors.

EVV and timekeeping records
