policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All employees, owners and anyone affiliated with the agency
policies.purpose: To set clear rules of conduct that protect consumers, keep relationships professional, and prevent financial dealings, undue influence and breaches of confidentiality.
policies.policy: No one affiliated with [AGENCY NAME] may assume power of attorney or guardianship over a consumer, and the agency does not require a consumer to endorse checks over to it (28 Pa. Code §611.57(b)). Staff do not give or receive gifts, loans or financial dealings with clients, as set out in CR-04. Staff keep client information confidential and use criminal history records only for hire, roster or retain decisions (28 Pa. Code §611.52(g)). Staff keep professional boundaries with clients and families at all times. Staff who commit a quality-of-care infraction are disciplined, and the discipline triggers an additional competency review under CMP-04 and PER-02. Violations of this policy lead to discipline up to and including termination, and to reporting to authorities where the law requires.

definitions.definition: The limit between a helpful working relationship and a personal, financial or other relationship that could harm the client or impair the worker's judgment.
A legal document that allows a person to act for another in financial or other matters.
A court-ordered arrangement in which a person is given authority over another person's affairs.
An owner, officer, employee, volunteer or contractor of the agency, and their immediate family members acting in connection with the agency.

procedures: At hire, each employee and owner receives the Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries rules. They sign an acknowledgment, and the Administrator files it in the personnel file (PER-03).

Staff may not accept appointment as agent under a power of attorney or as guardian, conservator or representative payee for any client. If a client or family member asks, the staff member declines politely and tells the Administrator the same day.
Staff may not ask a client to sign over or endorse checks to the agency or to staff. The agency bills payers and private-pay clients through the process in CR-06.

Staff may not borrow money, accept loans, buy or sell items, or share bank cards, PINs or account numbers with a client, and may not accept gifts, bequests or being named in a will, as set out in CR-04. A worker who is offered a gift reports it to the Administrator, who decides how to respond and records it.
Staff do not use a client's property, vehicle, phone or accounts for personal use. They do not take client items out of the home except as the service plan directs and the client allows.
Staff do not engage in romantic, sexual or exploitative relationships with clients. They do not discuss their own personal problems or religion or politics in ways that pressure the client.

Staff do not provide services outside the service plan or accept payment directly from a client or family for services. A client who asks for added services is referred to the supervisor to update the plan (SVC-03).

Staff do not connect with clients or their families on personal social media. They do not post photos or information about clients anywhere, and they do not take photos of clients without the client's written permission and the Administrator's approval.

Staff keep client information confidential at all times, including in conversations in public places and in electronic messages (CR-03). Information is shared only with those who need it to provide or manage care.

Staff access and use criminal history records only to decide whether to hire, roster or retain a person. They do not share them with anyone outside the agency except the Department of Health on inspection (CBC-03).

Staff report violations of this policy, including any attempt by another person to obtain a POA, a check endorsement or a gift, to the Administrator immediately. Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported under SAF-01.
The Administrator investigates each report within 5 business days and records the findings. The agency prohibits retaliation against anyone who reports in good faith.

When a worker is disciplined for a quality-of-care infraction, the Administrator records the discipline in the personnel file and schedules an extra competency review under CMP-04 and PER-02 before the worker returns to the affected tasks.

Violations of POA, guardianship, check endorsement, gift or exploitation rules result in discipline up to termination, and the Administrator makes any report to the Department of Health, law enforcement or Adult Protective Services that the law requires.
The Administrator reviews boundary issues at each annual training (PER-02) and the quality assurance review (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Enforces the policy, investigates reports, imposes discipline and schedules extra competency reviews.
Watch for boundary problems during supervisory visits and report them.
Follow the rules, decline prohibited requests, and report violations.

documentation: Signed Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries acknowledgment
Gift or request reports

Disciplinary records

policies.title: Client Records and Retention
policies.applies_to: Administrator, intake and supervisory staff, and all direct care workers
policies.purpose: To keep complete, secure client records that prove compliance with Chapter 611 and payer requirements, and make them available for Department of Health inspection.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a record for each client that includes the signed Consumer Information Packet acknowledgment, service plans and updates, visit notes and termination notices. The agency keeps on file documentation of compliance with the consumer protections in 28 Pa. Code §611.57, available for Department of Health inspection (28 Pa. Code §611.57(d)). Chapter 51 applies to licensed home care agencies (28 Pa. Code §611.4(b)), and the agency follows its record requirements. Records are kept in locked or access-controlled storage and protected under HIPAA (45 CFR 164.530) and CR-03. The retention period is set in this policy and confirmed against Chapter 51, Chapter 611 and OLTL and MCO contracts.

definitions.definition: All paper and electronic documents about a client's services, including intake, packet acknowledgment, service plans, visit notes, incident reports, complaints and termination notices.
A worker's record of each visit: date, times, tasks done, the client's condition and any change or incident.
The minimum time a record must be kept before it can be destroyed.
A review of agency records by the Pennsylvania Department of Health.

procedures: The Client Intake Coordinator opens a client record at intake (SVC-02). Each record is labeled with a unique client number and stored in locked cabinets or a password-protected, access-controlled electronic system.

The record includes: intake and eligibility information; the signed acknowledgment that the client received the Consumer Information Packet (CP-04, CP-05); the service agreement and rate disclosure (CR-06); the service plan and each update (SVC-03); and the client's consent forms and privacy notice acknowledgment.

Staff file in the record the documentation of compliance with the consumer protections in 28 Pa. Code §611.57, as listed in CP-06. This includes notice that no one affiliated with the agency holds power of attorney or guardianship and that the agency does not require check endorsement (CP-03).

Direct care workers write a visit note for every visit, on the same day, in the agency's required format. They sign or enter it electronically and turn it in by [SUBMISSION DEADLINE]. EVV records are kept with the visit notes (SVC-07).
Workers record any change in the client's condition, incident or concern on the visit note and report it to the supervisor as set out in SVC-08 and SAF-02.
Supervisors review visit notes at least [REVIEW FREQUENCY] and record supervisory visit results in the client record (SVC-04).
The Administrator files in the client record every written notice of discharge, transfer or termination, including the 10-day written notice and proof of delivery (CP-02).
Grievances, complaints and their resolutions are kept in the client record or a linked complaint log (CR-02). Incident reports are kept as set out in SAF-02.
Only staff who need the information to do their jobs may open a client record. The system or log records who accessed each record and when. Records are never left unattended in cars or public places.

Staff do not release client records to anyone except as the client has authorized in writing or as law allows, including to the Department of Health on inspection, and to OLTL, MCOs and other payers as contracts and HIPAA permit (CR-03).
Records are available to Department of Health inspectors on request during the inspection. The Administrator ensures that a staff member can retrieve any client record promptly and in complete form.

The agency retains client records for at least seven years after the last date of service, or any longer period required by Chapter 51, Chapter 611, an OLTL or MCO contract, or other law. The Administrator confirms the required periods with the Department of Health and each payer contract and extends this standard if a longer period applies.
When a client is discharged or services end, the Administrator closes the record, notes the date and moves it to archived storage with the same access controls.
Electronic records are backed up at least [BACKUP FREQUENCY], and the backup is stored securely. The Administrator keeps a written plan to restore records after a system failure or disaster.

At the end of the retention period, the Administrator authorizes secure destruction (shredding or secure electronic deletion) and records the date, method and records destroyed. Nothing is destroyed while an inspection, audit, legal hold or complaint is open.

Each quarter the Administrator audits a sample of client records for completeness, including the packet acknowledgment, plans, visit notes and termination notices. Results go to the quality assurance review (GOV-04), and gaps are corrected within 14 days.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees record keeping, access, retention, inspection readiness and destruction.
Opens records and files packet acknowledgments, agreements and compliance documents.
Review visit notes and file plan updates and supervisory visit records.
Write accurate, timely visit notes and protect client information.

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: Administrator, governing body/owners, Director of Operations or Clinical/Care Supervisor, Compliance Officer, office staff who prepare filings, and all direct care workers who must report incidents internally
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] gives the Pennsylvania Department of Health (the Department) every notice, report and filing that Chapter 611 and the Chapter 51 general provisions require, on time and in writing, and keeps proof of each submission. These obligations are license renewal, advance notice of new or discontinued services, immediate notice of serious noncompliance, reportable incidents, and changes in ownership or management.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will file all required reports with the Department accurately, in writing, and within the required time. The Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], is responsible for all state filings. A designated alternate, [ALTERNATE ADMINISTRATOR NAME], acts when the Administrator is unavailable. No filing is delayed because of staff absence, internal review or a pending investigation. (1) License renewal: the agency submits its renewal at least 60 days before license expiration, with the $100 non-refundable fee, and prepares for the Department's inspection before renewal (C3). (2) New or discontinued services: the agency gives the Department written notice at least 60 days before it begins a health care service it has not previously provided, and at least 60 days before it ceases an existing service (C32). (3) Serious noncompliance: if the agency knows it is out of compliance in a way that seriously compromises quality assurance or patient (client) safety, it notifies the Department immediately in writing, stating the reason and the corrective steps (C33). (4) Reportable incidents: the agency reports to the Department the events listed in the Chapter 51 notification provisions, namely deaths under unusual circumstances, medication-error deaths or serious injuries, hospital transfers resulting from injury or accident, abuse complaints, rape, disaster disruptions, loss of vital utilities, and unlicensed practice, within the timeframe stated in the full regulation text (C34). The Administrator confirms that timeframe against the current regulation and enters it on the Regulatory Calendar. (5) Change in ownership or management: the agency notifies the Department and obtains any required approval before the change takes effect. A change of ownership of 5% or more requires Department approval before it occurs (C35). The Administrator confirms current notice requirements for changes in management against the full text of the section before acting. This policy has no items assigned from an official Department checklist. It implements the reporting duties in the cited sections.

definitions.definition: The Pennsylvania Department of Health, Bureau of Health Care Facilities and Home Care Services, Division of Home Health, which licenses and inspects home care agencies under 28 Pa. Code Chapter 611.
A condition the agency knows exists in which it is out of compliance with a licensing requirement in a way that seriously compromises quality assurance or client safety.

An event on the Department's notification list: unusual-circumstance death; medication-error death or serious injury; hospital transfer from injury or accident; abuse complaint; rape; disaster disruption; loss of vital utilities; or unlicensed practice.
A transfer of the agency or of an ownership interest that triggers the Department's change-in-ownership requirements. A transfer of 5% or more requires Department approval before it occurs.
The agency's controlled tracking document listing license expiration, renewal due date, inspection preparation dates, reporting deadlines and notice periods, kept by the Administrator.
A dated written submission to the Department by the method the Department directs (online portal or email), with the agency retaining a copy and proof of transmission.

procedures: The Administrator maintains the Regulatory Calendar. It records the license expiration date, the renewal due date (60 days before expiration), the target internal renewal date (90 days before expiration), and the dates of any pending notices. The Calendar is reviewed at each monthly management meeting.

Renewal: At least 120 days before license expiration, the Administrator reviews the renewal requirements on the Department's home care webpage and confirms the current submission method. The Department accepts applications online only, so the Administrator does not mail or email a renewal unless the Department directs otherwise in writing.

Renewal: The Administrator completes the renewal form and pays the $100 non-refundable fee. Both must be submitted at least 60 days before expiration, and the agency's internal goal is 90 days. The Administrator saves the confirmation or receipt in the License file the same day.

Renewal: Before the Department's pre-renewal inspection, the Administrator conducts a self-review of the Chapter 611 requirements (see GEN-01, GEN-02). The review covers direct care worker files, consumer information packets, competency records, and the posted and retained license. Gaps are corrected and documented on a corrective action log. The Administrator is available to the inspector, and the agency keeps the inspection report and any plan of correction.

New services: Before the agency starts any health care service it has not provided before (for example, a new type of service or a new line of service), the Administrator prepares a written notice to the Department describing the service and the planned start date. The notice is submitted at least 60 days before the start. The agency does not advertise, accept clients for or deliver the service until the 60 days have run and any Department response has been addressed. The Administrator records the earliest permitted start date on the Regulatory Calendar.

Discontinued services: Before the agency stops any existing service or closes, the governing body approves the decision and the Administrator submits written notice to the Department at least 60 days before the service ends. Affected clients receive the written notice and transition help required by CP-02 and SVC-06, and payers and Medicaid managed care organizations are notified as their contracts require.

Serious noncompliance: Any employee who learns of a condition that may seriously compromise client safety or quality assurance (for example, workers placed without required clearances or competency, or a lapse in required supervision) reports it to the Administrator the same day.

Serious noncompliance: The Administrator decides the same day, with the Compliance Officer where available, whether the condition meets the definition. If there is doubt, the Administrator treats it as serious and reports. The Administrator takes immediate steps to protect clients, such as removing a worker from service or suspending an assignment.

Serious noncompliance: The Administrator sends the Department written notice immediately, with the reason for the noncompliance and the corrective steps being taken. The notice is not held for a full investigation. The Administrator sends a supplemental written report when corrections are complete. Copies go in the Regulatory Reports file and into the QA/PI log (see GOV-04).

Reportable incidents: Caregivers and supervisors report any event on the Department's list to the Administrator by phone immediately and in writing on the incident form within 24 hours (see SAF-02, SAF-01). Abuse, neglect and exploitation are also handled under SAF-01, including any mandated reports to protective services.

Reportable incidents: The Administrator determines the same day whether the event is reportable to the Department. The agency submits its written report within the timeframe stated in the full Chapter 51 notification text, as confirmed on the Regulatory Calendar. If that text allows more time, the agency's internal standard is still to report as soon as the facts are confirmed, normally the same business day. The report states what happened, who was involved, the immediate actions, and follow-up.

Reportable incidents: The Administrator keeps an Incident Reporting Log that lists each event, the date and time discovered, the date and method of the Department report, any other agencies notified (e.g., payer, managed care organization, law enforcement, protective services), and the outcome. The QA committee reviews the log quarterly for trends.

Change in ownership: Before any sale, transfer or issuance of ownership interest, the owner notifies the Administrator and the governing body in writing. If the change involves 5% or more of ownership, the agency submits the required notice and application to the Department and does not complete the transaction until the Department's approval is received in writing.

Change in ownership or management: The Administrator obtains the full current text of the change-in-ownership and change-in-management provisions and the Department's current forms and instructions before drafting any notice or timeline. A change of Administrator or key management is reported to the Department as those provisions require and is reflected in agency documents (organizational chart, policies, client information packet, and website).

Change of location or ownership structure: The agency holds one license per physical location, with no branch offices, and a virtual office does not qualify. Before moving or opening any additional site, the Administrator contacts the Department's Division of Home Health to find out what notice or new application is required. Care is not delivered from the new site until the Department confirms.

For every filing, the preparer drafts it, the Administrator or alternate reviews it for accuracy and signs it, and a copy and proof of transmission are filed in the Regulatory Reports file within one business day. If the Department does not acknowledge a submission within [NUMBER] business days, the Administrator follows up by phone or email and documents the follow-up.

The Administrator keeps current Department contact information (Division of Home Health, (717) 783-1379, reconfirmed annually; online application questions at RA-dhhomehealth@pa.gov; general inquiries at ra-dhhlicenquestions@pa.gov). Contact information is verified at each annual policy review (see GOV-03).

The governing body receives a report of all Department filings, inspection results and open corrective actions at each of its meetings. Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually, with attention to the duty to report incidents and noncompliance internally without delay (see PER-02). Retaliation against any employee who reports is prohibited.

responsibilities.duty: Approves new or discontinued services and any ownership change. Notifies the Administrator in writing before any ownership transfer. Reviews state filings and inspection results at each meeting.
Owns all Department filings. Maintains the Regulatory Calendar, submits the renewal and fee on time, decides what is reportable, signs and sends notices, and keeps proof of every filing.
Carries out the Administrator's reporting duties during absences so that no deadline is missed.
Advises on whether a condition is serious noncompliance, audits the Regulatory Calendar and filings quarterly, and tracks corrective actions to completion.
Escalates incidents and client-safety concerns to the Administrator the same day and supports client transition when services end.

required_items.text: A current copy of Chapter 611 must be maintained at the home care agency or registry.

Comply with applicable environmental, health, sanitation and professional licensure standards required by Federal, State and local authorities. Chapter 51 (general health-facility provisions) also applies under §611.4(b).
Before hiring or rostering a direct care worker: conduct a face-to-face interview with the individual.

Before hiring or rostering: obtain at least two satisfactory references. A satisfactory reference is positive and verifiable (verbal or written) from a former employer or other unrelated person who affirms the individual's ability to provide home care services.
Before hiring or rostering: require the individual to submit a criminal history report (per §611.52) and a ChildLine verification, if applicable (per §611.53).

Direct care worker files must document the date of the face-to-face interview and the references obtained. They must also hold the information required by §§611.52 and 611.53 and, if applicable, §§611.54, 611.55 and 611.56.
Require each direct care worker applicant to submit a criminal history report obtained at application or within the preceding 1 year. Office staff applicants and the owner(s) must also obtain one.
If the individual has been a PA resident for the 2 years before the request, they must request a State Police criminal history record.
If not a PA resident for those 2 years, the individual must obtain a Federal criminal history record and a Department of Aging letter of determination (per 6 Pa. Code §15.144(b)).

The agency or registry may request proof of residency, shown by any one of these: motor vehicle records; housing records; public utility records; local tax records; a signed income tax return with preprinted name and address; or employment records, including unemployment compensation records.

Prohibition: do not hire, roster or retain an individual if the State Police record shows a prohibited conviction listed in 6 Pa. Code §15.143, or if the Department of Aging letter says the individual is not eligible for hire or roster.

Records: keep files for direct care workers and office staff with copies of State Police records or Department of Aging letters, and keep owners' criminal history reports. All must be available for Department inspection.
Confidentiality: keep criminal history information confidential and use it solely to decide eligibility to be hired, rostered or retained.

Opportunity to appeal: if a decision not to hire, roster or retain rests wholly or partly on these records, give the individual information on how to appeal to the record sources if they believe the records are in error.

Exceptions: no new report is required for a worker who has complied and transfers to another agency or registry owned and operated by the same entity, or whose employer undergoes a change of ownership.
An agency or registry that serves persons under 18 must require each direct care worker applicant and each office staff applicant to request a ChildLine verification.
Prohibition: do not employ, roster or retain an individual whom ChildLine verifies as named in the Statewide Central Register as the perpetrator of a founded or indicated report of child abuse.
Records: keep ChildLine verification copies in the file of each employee, rostered individual and office staff member, and keep owners' copies. All must be available for Department inspection.

Provisional hiring is permitted only if the applicant has applied for a criminal history report and ChildLine verification, as applicable, and has given the agency or registry a copy of the completed request forms.
The agency or registry has no knowledge that would disqualify the applicant under 18 Pa.C.S. §4911.
The applicant swears or affirms in writing that they are not disqualified under Chapter 611.
Do not assign or refer the provisional hire until the §611.55 competency requirements are met.
Monitor the provisional hire awaiting a criminal background check through random direct observation and consumer feedback, and document the results in the individual's file.
Directly supervise, or assign another direct care worker to accompany, a provisional hire awaiting child abuse clearance who will serve a consumer under 18.
Provisional hire may not exceed 30 days for an individual who has been a PA resident for 2+ years, or 90 days for one who has not.

Termination: if the reports show disqualification, or the individual fails to provide the ChildLine verification or criminal history report within the provisional period, terminate the individual or remove them from the roster immediately.

Before assigning or referring a direct care worker, ensure the worker has either: (1) a valid PA nurse's license; (2) passed an agency/registry-developed competency examination meeting (b) and (c); or (3) completed one of these: (i) an agency/registry or other-entity training program meeting (b) and (c); (ii) a home health aide program meeting 42 CFR 484.36; (iii) the Department of Education nurse aide certification and training program; (iv) a training program meeting the standards of a Medicaid Waiver or other publicly funded HCBS program the agency participates in; (v) another program the Department identifies.
Competency exam/training must address at minimum: Confidentiality.
Consumer control and the independent living philosophy.
Instrumental activities of daily living.
Recognizing changes in the consumer that need to be addressed.
Basic infection control.
Universal precautions.
Handling of emergencies.
Documentation.
Recognizing and reporting abuse or neglect.
Dealing with difficult behaviors.
For direct care workers who will provide personal care, the exam/training must also address: Bathing, shaving, grooming and dressing.
Hair, skin and mouth care.
Assistance with ambulation and transferring.
Meal preparation and feeding.
Toileting.
Assistance with self-administered medications.

Document each worker's satisfactory completion of competency requirements in the worker's file. Keep a copy of any nurse or other health-professional license or certification. Documentation transfers between agencies/registries if the break in employment or roster status does not exceed 12 months.

Document in the worker's file a review of competency to perform assigned duties (direct observation, testing, training, consumer feedback, other Department-approved method, or a combination). Do it at least once per year after initial competency, and more often when discipline or other sanction (e.g., verbal warning or suspension) is imposed for a quality-of-care infraction.

Before consumer contact, each direct care worker and any other office staff or contractor with direct consumer contact must provide documentation of screening for, and freedom from, active mycobacterium tuberculosis. Screening follows CDC guidelines, and the documented screening date may not be more than 1 year before the start date.
Require those individuals to update the TB documentation at least every 12 months (counted from the last evaluation) and keep it in the individual's file.

Consumer right: to be involved in the service planning process and to receive services with reasonable accommodation of individual needs and preferences, except where the direct care worker's health and safety is at risk.

Consumer right: to receive at least 10 calendar days' advance written notice of intent to terminate services. Shorter notice is allowed if the consumer, despite notice, has failed to pay and is more than 14 days in arrears, or if the direct care worker's health and welfare is at risk.

Prohibitions: no one, by reason of their affiliation with the agency or registry, may assume power of attorney or guardianship over a consumer. The agency or registry may not require a consumer to endorse checks over to it.
Before services begin, give the consumer, legal representative or responsible family member an easy-to-read information packet containing items (c)(1)–(c)(7) below.
Packet item: a listing of the available home care services that will be provided by the direct care worker, and the identity of the worker who will provide them.
Packet item: the hours when services will be provided.
Packet item: fees and total costs for the services on an hourly or weekly basis.
Packet item: who to contact at the Department for information about licensure requirements and for compliance information about the particular agency or registry.
Packet item: the Department's complaint Hot Line (1-800-254-5164) and the telephone number of the local Area Agency on Aging Ombudsman Program.
Packet item: the hiring and competency requirements applicable to direct care workers employed by the agency or referred by the registry.

Packet item: a disclosure, in the format published by the Department in the Pennsylvania Bulletin, on the worker's employee vs. independent-contractor status and the resulting tax, insurance and other obligations of the consumer and the agency or registry.
Keep documentation on file at the agency or registry showing compliance with §611.57, available for Department inspection.

official.notes:
1) No single official 'policy checklist' was retrievable. Chapter 611 has no plan-of-operation or written-policy-list section. Its operational content is §§611.51–611.57 (the 'Governance and Management' subchapter), which is why the items above follow those sections. Chapter 51 also applies under §611.4(b), but I did not fetch it, so its policy requirements are not listed.
2) How DOH expects submission: licensure is by application to the Division of Home Health with a $100 fee per location (§611.2). DOH inspects before an initial license and before renewal (§611.2(a)). A copy of Chapter 611 must be kept on site (§611.4(a)). The change-of-ownership packet requires a signed 'Attestation of Policies and Procedures Compliance' naming the manual(s) that define the entity's policies.
3) Unverified, from secondary sources only: DOH takes applications online only since Mar. 31, 2026. The Jan. 14, 2021 application packet says to label exhibits, submit a checklist, and include 'required policies'. That packet says deficient applications get 30 days to resubmit revised policies. Third-party consultants organize manuals as exhibits tracking §§611.51–611.57. This is not an official format, so use the section order above, number each policy to the cited section (e.g., 611.52(h)), and confirm the current application and checklist with DOH (ra-dhhomehealth@pa.gov).
4) Medicaid PAS (CHC/OBRA Waiver) enrollment is outside Chapter 611, and I did not review it. Those programs may require additional written policies (e.g., incident reporting, EVV, abuse/neglect). Do not treat this list as complete for Medicaid participation.
5) The 'text' fields are condensed paraphrases of the regulation, not verbatim quotations. The item_id and cite values follow the document's own numbering.
